q: A replicated service's task is not rescheduled after its node reboots. What is the most likely cause?
options: A placement constraint no longer matches, or node availability is drain/pause
Swarm never reschedules tasks after reboots
The node lost its Raft log
The routing mesh removed the node
explain: Swarm reschedules failed tasks automatically. A task that stays missing points to scheduling: a placement constraint the node no longer satisfies, or node availability set to drain or pause. Check with docker service ps and docker node inspect.

q: A service update uses --update-failure-action rollback. New tasks fail their health checks. What happens?
options: Update pauses; old and new tasks run side by side
Swarm rolls the service back to the previous spec
Swarm retries the failed tasks forever
The service is deleted and recreated
explain: When an update exceeds the allowed failure ratio, the configured failure action runs. With rollback, Swarm reverts the service to its previous specification; pause would leave a mixed old/new state instead.

q: True or false: If two of three Swarm managers fail, running worker tasks stop serving traffic.
explain: False. Losing two of three managers loses Raft quorum, which blocks scheduling and cluster changes — but existing tasks on workers keep running and serving traffic.

q: An agent must run on every Swarm node, including nodes added later. Which service mode?
options: Replicated with --replicas set to the node count
explain: Global mode places exactly one task on every eligible node, including nodes that join later. A fixed replica count does not track cluster growth.

q: A Compose deploy: section works under docker stack deploy but is ignored by docker compose up. Why?
options: Both tools share the same state
deploy: is Swarm-only; Compose up ignores it
explain: The deploy: section (replicas, placement, resources) is honored only by docker stack deploy in Swarm mode. docker compose up silently ignores it.

q: Which sequence drains worker3 for patching, then returns it to service?
options: docker node rm, patch, then rejoin the swarm
node update --availability drain, patch, then --availability active
Scale every service to zero, patch, scale back
explain: Draining moves the node's tasks elsewhere without removing it from the cluster. Setting availability back to active afterward lets the scheduler place tasks on it again.

q: Service tasks stay Pending despite free cluster CPU and memory. What is the most likely cause?
options: The overlay network is out of IPs
A placement constraint matches no available node
The routing mesh blocks task startup
Global mode has too many nodes
explain: Pending means the scheduler found no eligible node. A constraint such as node.labels.disk == ssd matches nothing when no node carries that label — docker service ps shows the scheduling error.

q: Which command pins a service to nodes labeled disk=ssd?
explain: Constraints filter eligible nodes at scheduling time. node.labels are set with docker node update --label-add; engine.labels are daemon labels and node.hostname matches hostnames, not labels.

q: How do you rotate a Swarm secret used by a running service?
options: Edit it in place with docker secret update
Delete and recreate it under the same name
Pass the new value as an environment variable
Create a new secret, then service update --secret-rm/--secret-add
explain: Swarm secrets are immutable and cannot be deleted while in use. Rotation means creating a new secret and swapping it into the service with docker service update, which restarts the tasks.

q: Which statement about MKE control-plane placement is correct?
options: MKE's web UI listens on port 2377
Controllers run the MKE/Swarm/Kubernetes control planes; keep app workloads off them
Each MKE role needs a dedicated physical server
explain: MKE installs its control plane as containers on manager (controller) nodes. Running application workloads on controllers risks starving the control plane, so production clusters keep them separate.

q: An MKE backup was created with --passphrase, and the passphrase is lost. What is the consequence?
options: Only the admin password must be reset
Any passphrase works at restore time
The backup is unrestorable — it encrypts Swarm state and access control
Backups are unencrypted; the passphrase is cosmetic
explain: The passphrase encrypts the MKE backup archive. Without it, the Swarm state, configs, and access-control data inside cannot be recovered — store passphrases in a vault.

q: True or false: --opt encrypted also encrypts BRIDGE-network traffic between containers on one host.
explain: False. --opt encrypted is an overlay-driver feature: it enables IPsec on the VXLAN data path between nodes. Bridge networks have no such option — encrypt single-host traffic at the application level (TLS).

q: A service publishes 8080:80 swarm-wide. A client connects to a node running no tasks. What happens?
options: Request succeeds via the ingress routing mesh
Connection refused — only task nodes listen
It succeeds only on manager nodes
It is forwarded to a random local container
explain: The ingress routing mesh makes every node listen on the published port and routes the connection to a healthy task. Any node can accept traffic for the service.

q: A service must give clients direct task IPs instead of the default virtual IP. Which option?
options: Switch the service to global mode
explain: endpoint-mode dnsrr makes DNS return the individual task IPs instead of one virtual IP, so clients connect to tasks directly. The default vip mode load-balances behind the VIP.

q: Two of five Swarm managers are being decommissioned. What is the correct procedure?
options: docker node rm both; Raft reconfigures itself
Shut both down at the same time
Demote one at a time, checking quorum, then remove
Promote two workers, then remove both at once
explain: Manager changes must preserve Raft quorum. Demote managers one at a time and verify the cluster stays healthy between steps, keeping an odd manager count.

q: In Swarm deploy resources, what distinguishes limits from reservations?
options: Limits cap usage; reservations guarantee a minimum for scheduling
Reservations are hard caps; limits are soft
explain: Limits are hard ceilings a task cannot exceed. Reservations are the minimum resources the scheduler guarantees when deciding where a task can be placed.

q: MKE: QA needs read-only access to the production collection; release needs full control. How is this expressed?
options: Two Swarm secrets, one per team
Two grants binding each team to a role on that collection
One Scheduler grant covering both teams
Separate Linux users on each manager
explain: MKE access control is grants: subject + role + resource set. One grant gives the QA team View Only on the production collection; another gives the release team Full Control.

q: Why is pinning an app service to manager nodes with a constraint risky?
options: node.role accepts only the value worker
App workloads can starve Raft and widen the blast radius
explain: Managers run the Raft control plane. A hungry or compromised app task on a manager threatens cluster management itself, which is why managers are normally kept workload-free.

q: Which Swarm-to-Kubernetes mapping is correct?
options: Swarm service → Pod; stack deploy → compose up
Swarm service → Deployment; service scale → kubectl scale
explain: A Swarm service maps to a Kubernetes Deployment plus Service; docker stack deploy corresponds to kubectl apply -f, and docker service scale to kubectl scale.

q: docker swarm init on a two-NIC host omits --advertise-addr. Workers cannot join. Why?
options: The manager may advertise the wrong interface's address
Init binds all interfaces, so it must be a firewall
Workers can only join over the LAN interface
explain: On multi-homed hosts the manager can pick an unreachable interface to advertise. Set --advertise-addr explicitly to the cluster-facing address so join traffic reaches the manager.

q: A 20-replica rollout with --update-parallelism 1 --update-delay 30s is too slow. What should change?
options: These flags do not affect rollout speed
explain: Parallelism is how many tasks update per batch; delay is the wait between batches. Raising parallelism to 4–5 and shortening the delay speeds rollouts while still limiting blast radius.

q: Monitoring must run on every node; the web API needs 3 replicas on workers only. Which setup?
options: One service: global mode with 3 replicas
Agent with replicas equal to node count; web in global mode
explain: Global mode guarantees one agent task per node. The API uses a fixed replica count plus a node.role == worker constraint to stay off managers.

q: True or false: After a failed update with the default failure action, Swarm automatically rolls back all tasks.
explain: False. The default failure action is pause — the update halts in a mixed old/new state. Rollback happens only when failure_action is rollback or an operator runs docker service rollback.

q: Which Mirantis product names replaced UCP and DTR?
options: UCP → Docker Desktop; DTR → Docker Hub
explain: Mirantis renamed Universal Control Plane to Mirantis Kubernetes Engine (MKE) and Docker Trusted Registry to Mirantis Secure Registry (MSR).

q: A workload is Pending in Swarm and Kubernetes. What does it mean, and where do you check first?
options: The image is still pulling; just wait
The scheduler could not place it; inspect scheduling constraints and resources
Swarm means paused; Kubernetes means kubelet down
explain: In both orchestrators, Pending means the scheduler has not placed the workload. Check placement fit: docker service ps for constraint errors, kubectl describe pod for events such as insufficient resources or unmatched selectors.

q: A Dockerfile ends with CMD ["python", "app.py"]. What runs for docker run myimg python worker.py?
options: python app.py — CMD cannot be overridden
An error: CMD conflicts with arguments
explain: Arguments after the image name on docker run replace the CMD entirely (with no ENTRYPOINT set). The container runs python worker.py.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: A Dockerfile sets ENTRYPOINT ["/bin/backup.sh"] and CMD ["--full"]. What does docker run img --incremental execute?
options: An error: ENTRYPOINT takes no arguments
explain: ENTRYPOINT is fixed; CMD supplies its default arguments. Runtime arguments replace CMD, so the container runs /bin/backup.sh --incremental, and plain docker run img runs it with --full.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: Why does a shell-form ENTRYPOINT container take the full 10 seconds to stop, while exec form stops instantly?
options: JSON arrays parse faster than shell strings
Shell form makes /bin/sh PID 1, which does not forward SIGTERM
Shell form ignores docker stop by design
Both forms behave identically; it is random
explain: In shell form, PID 1 is /bin/sh -c, and the shell does not forward SIGTERM to the child process, so Docker waits out the grace period and SIGKILLs. Exec form makes the app itself PID 1, so it receives the signal directly.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: A build must download and unpack a 200MB dataset from an internal HTTP server. COPY or ADD, and why?
options: COPY — ADD is deprecated and blocks URLs
RUN curl — neither instruction fetches files
ADD — it fetches remote URLs and auto-extracts tarballs; COPY does neither
VOLUME — datasets never belong in images
explain: ADD has two features COPY lacks: downloading from a remote URL and auto-extracting local tar archives. For ordinary local files COPY is preferred, but it cannot fetch a URL at all.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: True or false: Copying source code BEFORE the dependency manifests keeps the install layer cached across code-only changes.
explain: False. Layer caching invalidates from the first changed instruction onward: COPY . changes on every edit and busts the install layer below it. Manifests first, install, then source — the install layer survives code-only changes.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: A Go image is 1.1GB but ships only a 25MB binary. Which build approach minimizes the production image?
options: Multi-stage build: compile in a builder, copy only the binary out
docker squash to merge the layers
.dockerignore the source from the final image
explain: A multi-stage build compiles in a full golang stage, then copies just the binary into a minimal runtime stage such as distroless or scratch. Toolchain and source never reach the production image.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: A Dockerfile contains three CMD instructions. Which one takes effect?
explain: Only the final CMD instruction in a Dockerfile is effective; earlier ones are silently discarded. Multiple CMDs usually signal a bad merge.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: docker images lists dozens of <none>:<none> entries after months of rebuilds. What are they, and what removes exactly them?
options: Dangling images — untagged leftovers whose tags moved to newer builds; docker image prune (no -a) removes exactly these
Corrupted images — remove them with docker rmi -f
Pulled-but-never-run images — docker container prune removes them
Duplicate tags — docker image dedupe cleans them up
explain: Every rebuild that moves a tag orphans the previous image: it keeps its layers but loses its name, surfacing as <none>:<none> — a dangling image. Plain docker image prune removes dangling images only; adding -a goes further and removes anything unused by a container. They are not corrupt, and container prune targets containers, not images.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: An ubuntu-based image for a static Go binary carries 40+ package CVEs. Best remediation?
options: Rebuild FROM scratch or distroless, dropping the unused OS packages
explain: The CVEs live in OS packages the static binary never uses. A scratch or distroless base removes that attack surface entirely instead of patching around it.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: Why must a registry password never be passed with ARG, and what replaces it?
options: ARG prints values in logs; use ENV
ARG values persist in image history; use BuildKit secret mounts
There is no risk with ARG
explain: ARG values are recorded in the image's build history, readable by anyone who pulls it. BuildKit --mount=type=secret makes the secret available during one build step without storing it in any layer.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: Pushes to an HTTP-only internal registry fail with 'server gave HTTP response to HTTPS client'. Client-side fix?
options: Add the registry to insecure-registries in daemon.json and reload
None — registries cannot run over HTTP
explain: The daemon refuses plain-HTTP registries unless they are listed under insecure-registries in /etc/docker/daemon.json. There is no per-push insecure flag.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: True or false: MSR promotion policies can block vulnerable images from production repositories, and garbage collection reclaims unreferenced blobs.
explain: True. MSR combines image scanning with promotion policies so only images passing vulnerability gates move to production repositories, and garbage collection deletes blobs and manifests no longer referenced.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST=1 is set and a developer pulls an unsigned tag. What happens, and what does DCT guarantee?
options: Pull is rejected; DCT guarantees provenance and integrity, not CVE-freeness
DCT scans the image for CVEs first
explain: Docker Content Trust uses Notary signatures: unsigned or tampered content is refused. It proves the image is what its publisher signed — it says nothing about vulnerabilities inside it.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: What does docker image prune -a remove, and what is the risk?
options: All images unused by any container, tagged included — rollback images can vanish
explain: prune -a deletes every image not referenced by a container, including tagged ones kept for rollback. The safer default prune removes only dangling images; use filters to protect keepers.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: A Dockerfile sets USER appuser, then a later apt-get fails with permission denied. Correct fix?
options: Install packages before the USER line, or switch back with USER root temporarily
sudo the apt-get inside the Dockerfile
Remove USER; builds must run as root throughout
explain: Instructions after USER run as that user, so package installs must happen earlier in the Dockerfile (or after a temporary USER root). Keeping USER appuser last preserves the non-root runtime.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: A container flips to unhealthy during traffic spikes while still serving requests. The HEALTHCHECK uses --timeout=5s --retries=3. Likely cause?
options: HEALTHCHECK status is stale after first run
unhealthy always means the app is down
The probe times out under load; it is too aggressive
explain: Under load the health endpoint answers slower than the 5-second timeout, and three failures mark the container unhealthy even though it serves traffic. Loosen interval/timeout/retries or lighten the endpoint.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: Which image reference should a production Swarm service use for a verified build?
options: The :stable tag, always the newest green build
The ci-<sha> tag from the pipeline
explain: Tags are mutable and can be re-pointed between scheduling and task startup, mixing versions across tasks. A digest reference resolves the exact verified bits every time.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: True or false: Deleting files in a later Dockerfile layer reclaims the space they used in an earlier layer.
explain: False. Layers are additive and immutable: deleted files still exist in the layer that created them and only appear removed via a whiteout. Clean up inside the same RUN that creates the files, or use a multi-stage build.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: docker build --build-arg API_KEY=... bakes the key into one RUN step. Where is it exposed afterward?
options: In docker history / inspect metadata, to anyone who pulls the image
Nowhere; ARG values are never stored
explain: Build-time ARG values are recorded in the image's history and config metadata. Anyone with pull access can read the key — pass secrets with BuildKit secret mounts instead.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: Large image pushes fail with 'blob upload unknown' behind a corporate reverse proxy; small images succeed. Likely cause?
options: The proxy buffers or times out chunked blob-upload PATCH requests
explain: Registry blob uploads use chunked PATCH requests that some reverse proxies buffer or time out, breaking large uploads while small ones slip through. Check proxy timeout and buffering settings against the registry logs.
domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry

q: Why is membership in the docker group treated as root-equivalent?
options: It grants sudo for all commands
Members can mount the host root into a privileged container
Members see only their own containers
explain: The Docker API is root-equivalent: a group member can run docker run -v /:/host --privileged and read or modify the entire host filesystem as root.

q: A container's JSON log grew to 40GB under default daemon settings. What should have been configured, and where?
options: A cron job running docker logs --truncate
log-opts max-size/max-file for json-file in daemon.json — the default never rotates
explain: The default json-file driver grows without bound. Setting "log-driver": "json-file" with "log-opts": {"max-size": "10m", "max-file": "3"} in /etc/docker/daemon.json caps and rotates container logs.

q: True or false: With live-restore enabled, containers also survive a full HOST reboot.
explain: False. live-restore decouples containers from the DAEMON only — they keep running through daemon restarts and upgrades. A host reboot kills the kernel and everything on it; restart policies handle the comeback.

q: After switching the storage driver to devicemapper and restarting, all images and containers 'vanished'. What happened?
options: Each driver has its own backing store; the old store is untouched but invisible
Docker deletes data on driver change for safety
explain: Every storage driver keeps a separate backing store under /var/lib/docker. Switching drivers points Docker at a different, empty store — switch back and the original images and containers reappear.

q: Where do you configure a default DNS server for every container on a host?
options: A DNS instruction in each Dockerfile
docker network create --dns on every network
explain: The "dns" setting in daemon.json applies a resolver to all containers on the host unless overridden per container with --dns.

q: True or false: Swarm join tokens expire automatically after 24 hours.
explain: False. Join tokens stay valid until rotated. If one leaks, run docker swarm join-token --rotate worker (or manager) immediately — the old token stops working at once.

q: An MKE install uses --san app.mke.corp.example --san 10.0.0.10. What do the SANs do?
options: They list names/IPs embedded in MKE's TLS certificate
explain: SANs (Subject Alternative Names) go into MKE's TLS certificate. Clients connecting through any name or IP not listed get certificate errors.

q: Which ports must be open between Swarm nodes?
options: None; Swarm uses the SSH socket
explain: Swarm needs 2377/TCP for cluster management, 7946 TCP/UDP for gossip-based node discovery, and 4789/UDP for the overlay VXLAN data path. MKE adds 443 and 6443.

q: docker info lists the nvidia runtime. How does a container use the GPU?
options: GPUs attach automatically to all containers
Reinstall Docker with GPU support compiled in
explain: The listed nvidia runtime means containerd can use it on request: --runtime nvidia, or the device-request form --gpus all on supported setups.

q: You add a registry hostname to the host's /etc/hosts, but containers still cannot resolve it. Correct fix?
options: Use --add-host (or extra_hosts in Compose) per container
Bake the entry into the image
Restart the container to pick it up
Containers cannot use custom host entries
explain: Containers have their own network namespace and hosts file; they never read the host's /etc/hosts. --add-host name:IP injects the entry into the container's hosts file.

q: What does "icc": false in daemon.json change?
options: Nothing; it is a deprecated no-op
Default-bridge containers can no longer talk to each other directly
explain: icc controls inter-container communication on the default bridge. Setting it false isolates containers there (published ports still work), which breaks apps that rely on direct container-to-container traffic.

q: Why does a bind-mount-heavy Compose app misbehave on Docker Desktop for Mac but not on Linux?
options: Compose files are incompatible with Desktop
Desktop runs the Engine in a VM; mounts cross the VM boundary
Desktop does not support bind mounts
explain: Docker Desktop runs the Linux engine inside a lightweight VM. Bind mounts cross that boundary through a file-sharing layer, so performance and permission behavior differ from native Linux mounts.

q: docker commands fail with 'Cannot connect to the Docker daemon'. What is the correct check order?
options: Daemon running? Socket permissions (docker group)? DOCKER_HOST set correctly?
Downgrade the client to match the server exactly
explain: Work the chain: confirm the daemon is running (systemctl status docker), confirm the user can reach the socket (docker group or sudo), and check DOCKER_HOST is not pointing somewhere unexpected. Client/server version skew alone rarely blocks connections.

q: How do you send all container logs to Splunk from the daemon, and what is the trade-off?
options: A Splunk sidecar with --volumes-from on every container
Logging drivers are set per image at build time
Set log-driver splunk in daemon.json; docker logs may then return nothing locally
explain: Daemon-wide "log-driver": "splunk" with the URL and token in log-opts ships all container logs to Splunk. The trade-off: docker logs shows nothing locally, and a blocking driver mode can stall container startup when Splunk is unreachable.

q: Why must an MKE backup be test-verified instead of just created?
options: Verification is a compliance formality only
Backups cannot be verified at all
A bad passphrase or truncated archive is discovered only at restore time
explain: An MKE backup holds Swarm state, configs, and access control, encrypted with its passphrase. An untested backup — wrong passphrase on record, truncated file — fails exactly when you need it: during a restore.

q: True or false: Containers on the default bridge network can resolve each other by name through Docker's embedded DNS.
explain: False. The default bridge has no embedded DNS name resolution (legacy --link aside). Create a user-defined bridge network and attach both containers — name resolution works there automatically.

q: A monitoring agent must bind host ports directly with no NAT and see host interfaces. Which network mode?
options: --network host — it shares the host stack, at the cost of isolation
explain: Host networking gives the container the host's own network stack: no NAT, no port mapping, full interface visibility. The cost is zero network isolation — port conflicts and host traffic exposure.

q: Containers must look like physical LAN devices, each with its own MAC and DHCP-reserved IP. Which driver, and the catch?
options: overlay — it spans the LAN automatically
macvlan — needs promiscuous-mode support, and containers can't reach the host IP by default
host — containers inherit the host MAC
explain: macvlan gives each container its own MAC and LAN address, appearing as a physical device. Caveats: the parent interface must allow promiscuous mode, the container cannot reach the host's own IP by default, and platforms with MAC limits may need ipvlan instead.

q: What does docker run -P do differently from -p 8080:80?
options: -P publishes all EXPOSEd ports on random host ports
explain: -P publishes every port the image EXPOSEs, each on a random host port (check docker port). -p maps one specific host port to one container port deterministically.

q: An app hardcodes the database container's IP and breaks after compose down/up. What broke, and the durable fix?
options: The subnet changed; pin it with --subnet
Compose randomizes IPs by design; use host networking
Container IPs are ephemeral; use the service name via embedded DNS
explain: Recreated containers get new IPs. On user-defined networks, Docker's embedded DNS resolves container and service names, which stay stable across recreates — reference names, never IPs.

q: How can one container join two isolated networks as a gateway, live?
options: docker network connect for each network — it works on running containers
Only one --network is allowed at creation; use host mode
explain: docker network connect attaches a running container to additional user-defined networks, and disconnect works the same way — no recreate needed. The container then routes between the networks it joins.

q: A Swarm service on an overlay must send egress through a forward proxy. Where is the proxy configured?
options: In the overlay definition with --opt proxy
Swarm routes egress via the managers automatically
By publishing the proxy port with -p
explain: Overlay networks do no egress proxying. The application itself (or a sidecar) must honor proxy environment variables; NO_PROXY should list internal destinations to bypass it.

q: A new overlay fails with 'pool overlaps' against the ingress network's 10.255.0.0/16. What is the fix?
options: Create the overlay with an explicit non-overlapping --subnet
Restart the daemon to free the pool
Ingress and custom overlays cannot coexist
explain: The ingress (routing mesh) network already owns 10.255.0.0/16. A new overlay whose default subnet collides must be created with an explicit --subnet outside that range.

q: Overlay service tasks cannot reach a LAN database at 192.168.50.20, but default-bridge containers can. Most likely cause?
options: Overlays cannot route to external IPs
Only docker run containers can reach the LAN
The database firewall blocks overlays specifically
An overlay or ingress subnet overlaps 192.168.50.0/24 and misroutes the traffic
explain: If a Docker network's subnet overlaps the LAN range, traffic for the database is routed into Docker's networks instead of out to the LAN. Re-create the overlay with a non-overlapping --subnet.

q: True or false: --opt encrypted can encrypt traffic on a bridge network.
explain: False. --opt encrypted is an overlay-driver feature providing IPsec for VXLAN traffic between hosts. For containers on one host, encrypt at the application level with TLS.

q: A container joins frontend via docker network connect after starting on backend. Why does ping db now resolve from frontend?
options: DNS works only on the first network; this is a cached IP
The container has an interface per network, and embedded DNS registers its name on each
frontend routes to all other networks automatically
explain: Each network attachment gives the container its own interface, and Docker's embedded DNS registers the container name on every network it belongs to, so peers on either network can resolve it.

q: Overlay encryption causes high CPU on busy nodes. When is it worth keeping?
options: Switch everything to the default bridge
Overlay traffic is encrypted by default anyway
Keep it on untrusted underlays; use app-level TLS on trusted networks
explain: --opt encrypted adds per-packet IPsec overhead, which is real on busy nodes. It earns its cost where the underlay is untrusted (multi-datacenter, cloud); on a trusted underlay, TLS on sensitive flows is more granular.

q: What changes when you publish -p 127.0.0.1:8080:80 instead of -p 8080:80?
options: The port binds loopback only — reachable from the host, not the network
Nothing; localhost binding is the default
The port publishes inside the container only
explain: The address before the host port selects the bind interface: 127.0.0.1 exposes the port only to the host itself, while -p 8080:80 binds 0.0.0.0 and is reachable across the network.

q: On a user-defined bridge, a container pings 8.8.8.8 but cannot resolve google.com. Default-bridge containers resolve fine. Likely cause?
options: User-defined bridges have no DNS configured
A firewall blocks the embedded DNS path (127.0.0.11) from the bridge subnet
User-defined bridges do not support external DNS
explain: User-defined networks resolve through Docker's embedded DNS at 127.0.0.11, forwarded to the host's resolvers. Corporate firewalls that only permit approved DNS paths often block this; check FORWARD rules for the bridge subnet.

q: A Swarm service behind the routing mesh sees only internal IPs, but the app needs real client source IPs. Fix?
options: Source IPs are never visible to containers
Publish the port in host mode (--publish mode=host)
explain: The ingress routing mesh SNATs connections, so tasks see the mesh's internal address. Publishing with mode=host delivers the original client IP to the task, at the cost of one task per node for that port and no mesh balancing.

q: Why is mounting /var/run/docker.sock into a container flagged CRITICAL in audits?
options: The mount is read-only and harmless
Socket mounts work only on managers
The risk is log spam only
Socket access is full daemon control — effectively host root
explain: The socket is the daemon's API. Any process that can write to it can launch a privileged container mounting the host root, so a compromised socket-mounted container means a compromised host.

q: An app must bind port 80 inside its container with least privilege. Which run flags?
options: Run as root; capabilities do not cover ports
explain: Binding a privileged port needs only the NET_BIND_SERVICE capability. Dropping ALL capabilities and adding back just that one keeps the container otherwise capability-free; --privileged grants everything.

q: A web app runs as USER www-data but cannot write its root-owned uploads directory. Correct fix?
options: Mount the directory from a privileged volume
chown the directory to www-data in the Dockerfile before the final USER
explain: Fix ownership at build time: create and chown the directory as root earlier in the Dockerfile, then keep USER www-data. The app stays non-root and can write to a directory it owns.

q: Rank these for a production database password: ENV in image, docker run -e, Swarm secret. Which wins and why?
options: ENV in the image — it ships with the app
Swarm secret — encrypted in Raft, mounted only into granted services
explain: Swarm secrets are encrypted in the Raft log and delivered as read-only files under /run/secrets to granted services only. ENV bakes the password into image history forever, and run -e exposes it via docker inspect.

q: True or false: Swarm node certificates must be renewed manually every 90 days or nodes drop out.
explain: False. Swarm's built-in CA rotates node certificates automatically; the default expiry is 90 days (tunable via docker swarm update --cert-expiry), and renewal needs no operator action.

q: A regulated customer needs Swarm Raft logs encrypted at rest, with a key required at manager restart. Which feature?
options: Swarm autolock — losing the unlock key strands restarted managers
explain: Autolock encrypts the Raft log at rest; after a restart each manager needs docker swarm unlock before rejoining. The operational risk is the key itself: lose it and a restarted manager can never rejoin, so vault it.

q: An MKE user in the right LDAP group gets 'access denied' creating services in the production collection. Likely misconfiguration?
options: No grant binds their subject to a role on that resource set
MKE does not support LDAP groups
They need a privileged docker client
explain: MKE authorization is a chain: subject (the LDAP group) + role + resource set, joined by a grant. Group membership alone grants nothing until a grant binds it to a role on the production collection.

q: A registry is compromised and a malicious :latest is pushed. Defenses in place: digest pinning and DCT. Which catches it?
options: Digest pinning only works on private registries
DCT scans the image for malware
Digest pinning — pulls still resolve the known-good sha256; DCT refuses the foreign-signed tag
explain: A digest reference names exact bits: the attacker's push has a different digest, so deployments keep pulling the known-good image. DCT adds a second wall by refusing tags not signed by a trusted publisher.

q: True or false: A container run with --read-only cannot write anywhere, including --tmpfs mounts.
explain: False. --read-only freezes the image's root filesystem, but a --tmpfs mount is a separate RAM-backed writable directory — the standard scratch-space fix for read-only apps.

q: A backup tool needs the mount syscall but the vendor suggests --privileged. Least-privilege alternative?
options: Run the tool on the host instead
Add the tool to the docker group
explain: Grant only the blocked operation: a custom seccomp profile that allows the mount syscall, or the SYS_ADMIN capability if that is the gate. --privileged disables every isolation layer at once.

q: An auditor wants proof production images carry no critical CVEs; the pipeline has no checks. Minimal credible addition?
options: Scan once a year at audit time
Sign images with DCT as proof
Scan in CI and gate promotion on critical/high CVE policy
explain: Scanning (MSR, Docker Scout, or equivalent) finds the CVEs; a promotion policy that blocks critical/high findings enforces the result. Signing proves provenance, not vulnerability-freeness.

q: A Swarm manager's disk is stolen. Autolock was on. What does the thief get, and what must the team still do?
options: Everything — autolock only protects running processes
The Raft log stays unreadable; still rotate join tokens and audit exposed keys/logs
Nothing is at risk; no action needed
Rebuild the entire swarm from scratch
explain: Autolock encrypts the Raft log, so cluster state and secrets stay unreadable without the unlock key. The team must still treat the disk as exposed: rotate join tokens and audit anything else stored on it.

q: A CI runner container needs to spawn sibling containers, but socket-mounting is banned. Safer architecture?
options: Orchestrator Jobs with scoped credentials, or a dedicated isolated runner host
explain: Handing a container the daemon socket is handing it host root. Run jobs through the Swarm/Kubernetes API with a least-privilege service account or client certs, or isolate CI on a dedicated hardened host away from production.

q: True or false: docker exec runs its process as the container's configured USER by default.
explain: False. docker exec runs as root by default regardless of the image's USER; pass --user to match. It is also an escalation path worth remembering for anyone with Docker API access.

q: Which run configuration most reduces risk from untrusted third-party images?
options: Trust Hub scanning and run normally
Scan once, then run --privileged for compatibility
--read-only, --cap-drop ALL, non-root user, no-new-privileges, resource limits, isolated network
explain: Assume the image is hostile and layer containment: read-only filesystem, all capabilities dropped, non-root user, no-new-privileges, CPU/memory limits, and an isolated network with no daemon socket. No single control is enough alone.

q: A database uses -v /data/db:/var/lib/postgresql/data. Why is this bind mount fragile, and what's better?
options: It ties the container to one host's path and permissions; use a named volume
Nothing — bind mounts are recommended for databases
explain: A bind mount depends on a host path existing with the right ownership on every host, which breaks portability and Swarm scheduling. A named volume is Docker-managed, portable, and driver-backed.

q: A Swarm service's named-volume uploads 'vanish' after its task reschedules to a new node. Why, and the fixes?
options: Swarm deletes volumes on reschedule; use bind mounts
Named volumes do not work in Swarm
Volumes are node-local; pin the service or use a cluster-aware volume driver
explain: A local named volume lives on one node; the rescheduled task mounts a fresh empty volume on its new node while the data sits on the old one. Pin the service with a placement constraint, or use a shared-storage driver (REX-Ray, Portworx, cloud drivers) so the volume follows the task.

q: True or false: Data written to a tmpfs mount is synced to disk when the container stops.
explain: False. tmpfs is RAM-backed: nothing is ever written to disk, and the contents vanish when the container stops. For persistence use a volume or bind mount instead.

q: In a volume backup command, what do --volumes-from db and -v /backup:/backup each do?
options: --volumes-from copies the data into the backup image permanently
--volumes-from mounts db's volumes for reading; -v binds a host path for writing the archive
The command backs up the ubuntu image
explain: --volumes-from mounts the database container's volumes into the throwaway backup container so tar can read the live data. The bind mount gives that container a host directory to write the archive into.

q: docker volume ls shows dozens of 64-hex-character volume names. What are they, and how do you prevent them?
options: Anonymous volumes from VOLUME instructions; prevent with named volumes
explain: A Dockerfile VOLUME instruction with no explicit mount creates an anonymous (hex-named) volume at run time. They accumulate and leak; always run with named volumes and clean strays with docker volume prune.

q: Why does the DCA treat --mount as best practice over -v for volumes?
options: They behave identically in all cases
--mount is explicit and validated; typos fail loudly instead of silently creating wrong mounts
explain: With -v, a typo can silently create a new empty volume or an unintended bind mount. --mount's key=value syntax is validated up front, so mistakes error out instead of corrupting your storage layout.

q: A Kubernetes pod needs 10Gi of durable storage. Which object chain provides it?
options: The kubelet provisions storage from the image
explain: The pod requests storage through a PersistentVolumeClaim (size, access mode), which binds a matching PersistentVolume provisioned from a StorageClass. CSI drivers plug third-party storage into this chain.

q: True or false: A named volume is the right mount for injecting one host config file read-only.
explain: False. Single host files are injected with a BIND mount (:ro or readonly) mapping the file in directly. Named volumes are Docker-managed data stores, not a file-injection mechanism.

q: A Dockerfile has VOLUME /var/lib/mysql, and an unmounted run shows a hex-named volume in docker inspect. Why?
options: That directory is the image layer cache
Docker auto-creates an anonymous volume for the VOLUME path
explain: When no mount is given for a VOLUME path, Docker creates an anonymous volume so data persists outside the container's writable layer. Name it explicitly with -v dbdata:/var/lib/mysql to control it.

q: Can stock Docker split container layers onto an SSD and image storage onto an HDD? Honest answer?
options: Yes — symlink only /var/lib/docker/volumes to the HDD
Performance does not depend on storage layout
No — one --data-root; put it on the SSD or use volume drivers for tiering
explain: Docker has a single data root (/var/lib/docker) covering layers and image storage together. Mount the fast SSD there, use volume drivers or plugins for tiered data placement, and watch usage with docker system df.
docker service scale makes the same API call as update --replicas, so parallelism, delay, and update order all apply. It is a Swarm service command, not a Compose-only feature.
q: True or false: docker service scale web=5 is shorthand for docker service update --replicas 5 web, honoring update_config.

explain: The default stop-first order stops the old task before starting its replacement. start-first starts the new task first for zero downtime, but needs headroom for one extra task per batch — on a full cluster that is exactly the Pending stall.
options: --update-order start-first; it temporarily needs capacity for a seventh task
q: A 6-replica service fills its cluster exactly; updates stall with tasks Pending. Which change gives zero-downtime updates, and at what cost?

explain: --update-max-failure-ratio is the tolerated fraction of failed tasks before a rollout pauses; the default 0 pauses on the first failure. Parallelism and delay change rollout speed, not failure handling.
q: Which flag lets a 50-replica rollout keep going when a few tasks fail on bad nodes?

explain: --update-monitor is the per-batch observation window, and its default is only 5s. A task that dies at 45s passes a 5s monitor, so the rollout 'succeeds' and the failure surfaces later as restarts.
q: Updated tasks crash 45 seconds after starting, after the rollout already reported success. Which setting catches slow crashes like this?

explain: Stack deploy never builds — it silently ignores build: and expects every image to already exist in a registry reachable by all nodes. Build and push first (docker build / docker compose build, then docker push), then deploy.
q: True or false: docker stack deploy builds any images declared in the Compose file's build: section.

explain: Only secrets get Raft-log encryption; they mount under /run/secrets/<name> by default. Configs are stored unencrypted and mount under /<config-name>, so they must never hold sensitive material — that encryption boundary is the whole distinction.
q: True or false: Swarm configs are encrypted in the Raft log, just like Swarm secrets.

explain: A docker login lives only in that host's ~/.docker/config.json; workers never see the manager's session. --with-registry-auth (on service create or stack deploy) ships the credential with the task so workers can pull.
options: Run docker login manually on every worker
Deploy with --with-registry-auth so the manager forwards its credentials to workers
Copy the image tarball to each worker with docker save/load
q: Workers fail to pull a private image the manager pulls fine after docker login. What is the fix?

explain: --force-new-cluster bootstraps a new single-manager cluster from the survivor's Raft state, restoring services, networks, secrets, and configs. Fresh managers and workers can then join the rebuilt cluster.
options: Wait for Raft to elect the survivor
Run docker swarm join on the survivor
Run docker swarm init --force-new-cluster on the surviving manager
q: Two of three managers are permanently destroyed; the survivor holds Raft data but has no quorum. What is the recovery path?

explain: The default --restart-condition any restarts a task regardless of exit code, so run-to-completion jobs loop forever. Use on-failure (restarts only on non-zero exits) or none for batch work.
q: True or false: With the default restart condition, a one-shot task that exits 0 is left alone and not restarted.

explain: False. The bare service name resolves to the virtual IP; tasks.<service> is the special name that resolves to the individual task IPs in round-robin — what scrapers and sidecars use to reach each replica.
q: True or false: On an overlay network, tasks.<service> resolves to the service's VIP, like the bare service name.

explain: Placement preferences are soft distribution hints: spread=node.labels.az balances tasks across the label's values after hard constraints are applied. Unlike constraints, preferences never refuse to schedule a task.
options: Global mode, one task per node
A placement preference used as a hard filter
q: A service's tasks must spread evenly across nodes by their node.labels.az values. Which mechanism does this?

explain: Mount metadata (target name, uid, gid, mode) is set when the secret is granted to the service — the only place it can be controlled. Secrets mount read-only in an in-memory filesystem, so chmod at runtime cannot change them.
options: chmod the file inside the container at startup
Impossible — secrets always mount with default ownership
q: An app requires its mounted secret file at mode 0400, owned by root, under a custom name. How is that configured?

explain: kubectl rollout undo reverts the Deployment to its previous ReplicaSet revision, and rollout status watches progress. Kubernetes keeps revision history (default 10) precisely for this operation.

kubectl scale deployment to zero and back up
Kubernetes has no rollback; re-apply the old manifest

explain: maxUnavailable: 0 means the available count never dips below desired, while maxSurge: 1 allows one extra pod during the swap — the mirror of Swarm's start-first update order. It needs headroom for that one extra pod.
options: A DaemonSet instead of a Deployment
q: A Kubernetes Deployment must never drop below its full replica count during a rollout. Which strategy settings express this?

explain: False. Compose files merge in order with LATER files overriding earlier ones for the same keys — prod.yml wins. That rule is what makes the base-plus-environment-override pattern work.
q: True or false: In stack deploy -c base.yml -c prod.yml, base.yml wins conflicting keys because it is listed first.

explain: docker swarm unlock-key --rotate issues a new key and re-encrypts the Raft state in place; the old key stops working immediately. It is the standard response when a key holder leaves.
q: True or false: Rotating a Swarm unlock key requires reinitializing the cluster.

explain: --force triggers a fresh rolling update under the existing update_config even when nothing in the spec changed — the 'bounce the tasks' operation. Scaling to zero creates an outage window and abandons rolling discipline.
options: docker service scale web=0, then scale back up
docker service update --image with the same tag
docker service rm, then recreate the service
q: Running tasks hold stale config from an external store; no spec change is needed, only a re-roll. What is the cleanest command?

explain: Short-syntax depends_on waits only for the dependency's container to start, not for the process inside to accept connections. The long syntax with condition: service_healthy gates startup on the dependency's HEALTHCHECK actually passing.
options: depends_on is broken; add a sleep to the entrypoint
depends_on already waits for database readiness
Compose cannot order startup; move to Swarm
depends_on only orders container start; give db a healthcheck and use condition: service_healthy
q: With docker compose up, api crashes connecting to postgres despite depends_on: [db]. Why doesn't depends_on prevent it, and what fixes it?

Tag first: docker tag myimg:2.0 registry.internal:5000/team/myimg:2.0, then push that name

domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry
explain: False. save serializes the image itself — layers, tags, and history — and load restores it bit-for-bit. The flattening tool is docker export (container filesystem, no layers/history), a different command.
q: True or false: docker save strips an image's history and tags; load restores layers only.

domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry
explain: ARG values exist only during the build and are absent from the running container's environment. ENV is baked into the image config and present in the process at runtime — visible in docker inspect, so never use it for secrets.
options: ARG for the build-time version; ENV for the runtime hostname
ENV for both; ARG is deprecated
ARG for both; ENV is not visible at runtime

domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry
explain: Labels are first-class, queryable metadata: --filter label= matches them, and docker image inspect shows them per image. OCI-standard label keys exist precisely for this kind of traceability.
options: Grep the output of docker history
Labels are write-only and cannot be queried
q: Images carry their git commit in a label. How do you list local images built from one specific commit?

domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry
explain: EXPOSE is documentation metadata only — it publishes nothing. A port becomes reachable from outside only when explicitly published with -p or -P (or exposed through a Swarm service port).
q: True or false: An image declaring EXPOSE 6379 publishes port 6379 on the host when a container starts.

domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry
explain: --start-period is a grace window after container start during which probe failures do not count toward the unhealthy threshold. Interval, timeout, and retries tune the steady-state probe; none of them grant startup grace.
q: A service's HEALTHCHECK fails during its 90-second warmup, rolling back updates. Tuning interval, timeout, and retries didn't help. Fix?

domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry
explain: False. The auth field is base64 ENCODING, not encryption — it decodes to username:password in one step for anyone who can read the file. A credential helper (credsStore) keeps the secret out of the file entirely.
q: True or false: After docker login, the auth field in config.json is encrypted with the user's keychain key.

domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry
explain: Immutable tags are enforced server-side: once a tag exists, any push that would replace it is rejected, so the bad CI run fails loudly. Content Trust verifies signatures; it does not freeze tags.
q: A buggy CI run overwrote an MSR release tag and poisoned production pulls. Which registry feature prevents tag overwrites?

domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry
explain: False. --no-cache ignores the layer cache but still builds on the LOCALLY cached base image. Refreshing the base is --pull's job — the FROM layer is otherwise reused without contacting the registry.
q: True or false: docker build --no-cache also fetches a newer base image from upstream.

domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry
explain: Build cache is accounted separately from images, so image prune leaves a full disk full. docker builder prune is the dedicated command, and --filter until= lets you keep recent cache while reclaiming the rest.
q: True or false: docker image prune also reclaims the space held by BuildKit build cache.

domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry
explain: ADD's two conveniences have different scopes: it fetches remote URLs but auto-extracts only tar archives from the local build context. For a remote tarball, download and unpack explicitly with curl and tar in a RUN step.
options: ADD auto-extracts only local tar archives; remote URLs download as-is — fetch and extract in a RUN step
The URL needs a trailing slash to trigger extraction

domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry
explain: False. Layers form a parent chain; deleting a base out from under its children would orphan them, so the daemon refuses. Remove or rebase the children first (-f forces it, leaving dangling parents).
q: True or false: docker rmi freely deletes a base image even while child images still depend on it.

domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry
explain: A plain push uploads a single-architecture image. A manifest list wraps one manifest per architecture under a single tag, so each host's daemon automatically selects its native variant.
options: x86 hosts pull ARM images with --privileged
ARM images can never leave ARM hosts
They publish a multi-arch manifest list, built with docker buildx --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64

domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry
explain: False. Relative WORKDIR paths resolve against the PREVIOUS WORKDIR, exactly like shell cd — the steps run in /app/src. Only an absolute WORKDIR resets the path.
q: True or false: WORKDIR /app followed by WORKDIR src puts subsequent RUN steps in /src.

domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry
explain: The build context is tarred and shipped to the daemon on every build, and changes in it bust the COPY layer cache. .dockerignore keeps build-irrelevant files out, speeding transfers and stabilizing the cache.
options: Buy a faster disk for the daemon host
Build with --no-cache to skip sending the context
Add a .dockerignore excluding node_modules, .git, and test data
q: Every build spends 3 minutes 'sending build context' — the context is 4GB including node_modules and .git. What is the fix?

explain: False. The daemon fails fast on malformed config and refuses to start; journalctl -u docker shows the exact parse error. A trailing comma after a daemon.json edit is the classic cause.
q: True or false: Invalid JSON in daemon.json is ignored — the daemon starts with defaults and logs a warning.

explain: dockerd is a systemd service and never inherits shell environment; its variables come from systemd. Set them in a drop-in (e.g. docker.service.d/http-proxy.conf), then daemon-reload and restart — and keep internal registries in NO_PROXY.
options: As ENV instructions in each Dockerfile
In a systemd drop-in setting HTTP_PROXY/HTTPS_PROXY/NO_PROXY for docker.service
q: docker pull times out behind a corporate proxy, though curl with proxy variables works. Where do the daemon's proxy settings belong?

explain: "bip" sets the address of the docker0 bridge itself, moving it off the conflicting range. It only covers the default bridge — user-defined networks are governed by default-address-pools.
options: Set "bip": "10.200.0.1/24" in daemon.json and restart the daemon
q: The corporate LAN uses 172.17.0.0/16, colliding with the docker0 bridge and breaking return traffic. What is the daemon-side fix?

explain: bip addresses only docker0. default-address-pools defines the supernets Docker subdivides when auto-assigning subnets to user-defined networks, which is the knob that ends pool-level collisions.
options: Widen bip; it covers user-defined networks too
"default-address-pools" in daemon.json, e.g. base 10.50.0.0/16 with size 24
q: User-defined networks keep grabbing subnets colliding with corporate ranges; bip is already set. What controls their address pool?

explain: Small packets pass but large ones vanish: classic path-MTU failure, where encapsulation overhead pushes frames past the tunnel MTU and the fragmentation-needed ICMP is filtered. Lowering the container MTU makes packets fit.
options: VXLAN is incompatible with VPN tunnels
An MTU black hole — set "mtu": 1400 in daemon.json so packets fit the tunnel
Raise the MTU to 9000 for jumbo frames
The VPN blocks Docker traffic specifically
q: Large transfers over a VPN tunnel hang while small requests succeed; LAN traffic is fine. Likely cause and fix?

explain: False. Remapping gives containers subordinate UID/GID ranges: container root maps to a HIGH, unprivileged host UID. An escaped process lands as that unprivileged user, not host root.
q: True or false: With userns-remap enabled, container root (uid 0) maps to host root for volume files.

explain: Contexts make the target explicit, named, and inspectable (docker context ls) before every command. DOCKER_HOST is invisible ambient state — one stale export silently retargets every command in the shell.
options: docker context: named endpoints, switched with docker context use and always visible
Run each daemon on a different TCP port
DOCKER_HOST is the only supported remote method

options: Append :z (shared) or :Z (private) to the bind mount so it is relabeled

q: True or false: A Windows Server Core image can run on a Linux host because containers carry their own kernel.

explain: Plugins are first-class daemon extensions: docker plugin install fetches and enables the plugin once you grant its requested permissions. Its driver name then works anywhere volumes are created.
options: Volume drivers must be compiled into the daemon
Through the host package manager only
Copy the plugin binary into every container
docker plugin install <vendor>/<plugin>, then docker volume create --driver <plugin>

Put HTTP basic auth in front of the daemon

q: True or false: The "bip" setting in daemon.json also controls the subnet of the docker_gwbridge network.

explain: True. Driver scope matters: bridge/host/null are local to one daemon; overlay is swarm-scoped. Same name on two hosts is two networks, and --attachable is an overlay concept, not a replication mechanism.

Only affects its own processes; harmless

A grant binding the service account to the Scheduler role on /Production — Scheduler deploys and manages services without cluster-admin rights
Stack more View Only teams — memberships accumulate
Restricted Control is the CI/CD role

explain: True. Task history retention is a swarm-level setting, default 5, raised with `docker swarm update --task-history-limit`. There is no per-service --history-retain flag and no ps escape hatch; manager count affects quorum, not retention.
q: True or false: service ps history length is the swarm-wide --task-history-limit (default 5), set via swarm update.

explain: Availability has three states: active (normal), pause (no new tasks, existing keep running), drain (existing tasks are shut down and rescheduled elsewhere). There is no --force on node update, and kubectl drain is a different orchestrator entirely.
options: pause only stops NEW scheduling — existing tasks stay put; drain (docker node update --availability drain) gracefully shuts tasks down and reschedules them
q: Node paused before patching, but its 12 tasks never migrated. What went wrong, and the right command?

explain: True. --force-new-cluster is the disaster-recovery path: it forces the local node to become a single-manager swarm from its Raft data, discarding the lost managers — the same mechanism as item 305's scenario. q: True or false: After losing quorum, swarm init --force-new-cluster on the survivor rebuilds a single-manager cluster from its Raft state.

explain: True. Raft quorum = majority: 3 of 5. The minority side goes read-only; the majority side keeps working. Losing one more on the majority side leaves 2/5 — no quorum anywhere, so no new scheduling (running tasks keep running) until quorum is restored.
q: True or false: In a 5-manager swarm split 3/2, the 3 side keeps scheduling; losing one more manager halts scheduling cluster-wide.

q: Replicas pile into one AZ though nodes are labeled az=1a|1b|1c. Which placement setting spreads them?

explain: True. --rotate generates a new join token for that role and revokes the old one; cluster membership is unaffected since tokens are only checked at join time — the same response as item 503's leaked-token scenario. Manager tokens don't parent worker tokens.

explain: Two different label stores: daemon.json labels → engine.labels.* (per-engine config); docker node update --label-add → node.labels.* (swarm spec, visible in node inspect). The constraint names the node-label namespace the admin never populated; SIGHUP doesn't move labels between stores.

daemon.json labels need a com.docker. prefix
Constraints only match engine labels now

explain: docker service logs aggregates every task's stdout/stderr in one stream. service ps has no --logs flag; manual SSH scales terribly and misses rescheduled tasks; docker logs works on standalone containers AND service task containers — the point is aggregation.

SSH to each node, docker logs per container
docker logs needs a logging plugin first

explain: True. Constraints filter the candidate set for ANY mode, including global — the scheduler places one task per node that passes the constraint. Replica math breaks when nodes join or leave, and Swarm does not honor Kubernetes taints.

explain: True. Swarm forbids demoting the final manager — zero managers means no Raft, no scheduler. Force-leaving it dissolves the swarm entirely: containers keep running on workers, but orchestration ends and nothing auto-promotes a replacement.
