q: True or false: Only a digest reference (app@sha256:...) is immutable — tags are mutable pointers that upstream can rebuild.

domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry
explain: True. save serializes images (tags, history, shared layers deduplicated) to a tarball; load restores them. export is for CONTAINERS — flat filesystem, no tags/history — and /var/lib/docker is not portable across hosts or storage drivers.
q: True or false: Air-gapped image transfer uses docker save -o bundle.tar (all images) and docker load at the destination.

domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry
explain: ENV persists in the image config — inspect shows it, history shows the assignment, and every derived image inherits it. ARG-only values passed via --build-arg don't persist, but the moment they're copied into ENV they do. The secret-mount pattern keeps the token out of all layers.
options: The developer — ARG values never appear anywhere
The reviewer — ENV bakes the value into the image config (docker inspect; history shows the assignment); use RUN --mount=type=secret so the token never lands in any layer
Tokens are encrypted at rest by BuildKit
q: Dockerfile: ARG NPM_TOKEN then ENV NPM_TOKEN=$NPM_TOKEN. A reviewer flags token recovery from the image. Who's right?

domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry
explain: True. ADD has two magic behaviors COPY lacks: auto-extracting local tarballs and fetching remote URLs. When you want the archive as a file, COPY is the precise tool. --no-extract is an invented flag, and the .tgz extension extracts the same way.
q: True or false: ADD auto-extracts local tar archives into the destination; to keep the tarball as a file, use COPY.

domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry
explain: Layers are additive: a delete in layer N+1 hides but never removes layer N's bytes. The fix is one RUN that downloads, builds, and cleans up before the layer commits. rm works fine inside builds — placement is the issue — and prune/squash are after-the-fact or experimental detours.
options: rm doesn't work in builds; image prune after
The cache still references it; builder prune
Each RUN is a layer; a later delete only whiteouts the file — the bytes remain in the earlier layer. Chain download+build+cleanup in ONE RUN so the SDK never lands in a committed layer
q: A later RUN rm -rf /sdk didn't shrink a 2.4GB image. Why, and what fixes it?

domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry
explain: imagetools inspect queries the registry and prints the manifest list with platforms/digests — the same check as item 422. docker inspect describes the LOCAL image only, history shows layer commands, and pulling to check is the wasteful fallback.
options: docker buildx imagetools inspect app:2.0 — lists the manifest's platforms without pulling anything
docker inspect shows the remote matrix
Pull it on an ARM host
q: Verify which architectures a published tag's manifest covers, before rebuilding. How?

domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry
explain: certs.d/<host>:<port>/ca.crt is the documented trust anchor for registries with private CAs — verification stays on. Both per-pull/per-login flags are invented, and plain HTTP exposes credentials as well as content.
options: Install the corporate CA into /etc/docker/certs.d/registry.corp:5000/ca.crt on every engine — TLS stays fully verified, against the corporate CA
Disable TLS; internal networks don't need it
q: Pulls fail x509 against a self-signed corporate CA; insecure-registries is banned. Proper fix?

domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry
explain: True. The registry is content-addressed: deleting a tag removes the manifest pointer, but blobs are shared and only freed by GC — which must not race with pushes, hence read-only/stopped. This restates item 421's finding; system prune cleans the daemon, not registry storage.
q: True or false: Deleted tags free no registry disk until garbage-collect runs (registry read-only or stopped).

domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry
explain: MSR's immutable tag rules evaluate at push time: an existing tag can't be repointed. Labels describe images and enforce nothing; --lock is invented; Content Trust verifies signatures rather than freezing tags.
options: Docker Content Trust freezes signed tags
MSR repository settings — the immutable-tags policy rejects pushes to a tag that already exists; promotion workflows must mint new tags
q: prod-* tags must reject overwrites at the registry after a bad overwrite incident. Where is this enforced?

domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry
explain: False. rmi untags first and deletes only when the reference count hits zero — with two tags on one image ID, one rmi just drops a name. Deletion happens when the LAST reference goes.
q: True or false: docker rmi on one of two tags for an image deletes the image and breaks the other tag.

domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry
explain: The default docker driver builds in-process and is single-platform; the docker-container driver runs real BuildKit with multi-platform support. --load is single-platform-only, QEMU alone doesn't change the driver, and the classic builder has no manifest-list support.
options: Create a docker-container driver builder (buildx create --driver docker-container --use) — real BuildKit in a container, with multi-platform support (plus QEMU for cross-arch)
q: buildx errors: the docker driver doesn't support multi-platform builds. What's the fix?

domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry
explain: scout quickview is the human-readable summary; scout cves is the detailed CVE list (with --exit-code for CI gates). docker scan (the Snyk integration) was removed, and scout --deep doesn't exist.
options: docker scout quickview app:2.0 — summarizes vulnerabilities and upgrade recommendations
q: A quick vulnerability/recommendation overview of an image — not a CI gate. Which command?

explain: True. live-restore: true keeps containers running across daemon restarts/upgrades — the old daemon hands them off (the same setting as item 335). Restart policies restart containers AFTER the daemon returns; false is the disabling value; Swarm services still restart their tasks.
q: True or false: live-restore: true in daemon.json keeps containers running across daemon restarts and upgrades.

explain: Dual-mode logging isn't a thing: the engine either keeps local logs (json-file/journald/local → docker logs works) or streams them away (remote drivers → docker logs errors). There is no logs --driver flag and no read: true log-opt.
options: Only json-file, journald, and local support docker logs reads — remote drivers (gelf, syslog, fluentd) are write-only from the engine's perspective; revert the default and ship with a forwarder sidecar if centralization is needed
A read: true key under log-opts
Logs cache locally for 24h; retry later
q: Default driver switched to gelf; docker logs now errors 'does not support reading'. Reality and fix?

explain: True. SIGHUP/systemctl reload applies a documented subset (debug, labels, insecure-registries, etc.) without restart; structural options like storage-driver/data-root need a full restart. The daemon does not watch daemon.json, and --debug on logs is a client display flag.
q: True or false: Daemon debug logging can be enabled without restart — set debug in daemon.json, then SIGHUP / systemctl reload.

explain: data-root only tells the daemon WHERE to look — it copies nothing. The safe move is stop → rsync → repoint → start (the same procedure as item 444). The daemon starts EMPTY on the new path if you skip the copy; a live symlink fights the running daemon.
options: Set data-root and restart — it migrates
Stop the daemon, rsync -a /var/lib/docker/ /data/docker/, set data-root in daemon.json, start — the engine never moves existing data for you
q: /var/lib/docker filled the root disk; a 500GB mount waits at /data. Safe migration procedure?

explain: True. AuthZ plugins are the engine's request-interception point: allow/deny per API endpoint and user. seccomp filters SYSCALLS inside containers, not API calls; MKE RBAC governs MKE-managed clusters, not a bare engine; docker-group membership is all-or-nothing API access.
q: True or false: Blocking docker exec for developers on a bare engine is done with an authorization plugin, not RBAC or seccomp.

explain: v2 plugins declare required privileges (network, mounts, devices) that must be granted at install; and a plugin lives on the node where it's installed — Swarm doesn't distribute it. Plugins DO work with Swarm services once installed everywhere, and --privileged is a container flag.
options: Two misses: plugins need privilege grants (--grant-all-permissions or interactive approval), and plugins are node-local — install on EVERY node that will run the workload, not just the manager
Plugins install cluster-wide; the name is misspelled
Volume plugins never work with Swarm
q: plugin install hangs on input; later, worker tasks fail 'plugin not found'. What two things went wrong?

explain: The graph driver reads only its own backend directory — switching drivers abandons the old tree (data intact on disk, unusable). Migration is backup → switch → restore. Nothing was deleted by overlay2, no migrate flag exists, and the driver is changeable with exactly this procedure.
options: Drivers aren't convertible in place — each keeps its own tree; the old data sits invisible under the devicemapper directory. Push/save images and back up volumes FIRST, switch, then re-pull/restore
q: Driver flipped devicemapper→overlay2; all images 'vanished'. What happened, and the correct migration?

explain: True. Containers get Docker's default ulimits (nofile ~1024 soft), not the host's; --ulimit sets them per container (or default-ulimits daemon-wide). Host sysctl doesn't propagate into containers, and --pids-limit caps processes, not descriptors.
q: True or false: A container's nofile starts at Docker's conservative default (~1024), raised with --ulimit nofile=65536:65536.

explain: --memory-swap is the TOTAL (RAM+swap) allowance; equal to --memory leaves no room for swap — the same equality rule as item 471. -1 means UNLIMITED swap; disabling the OOM killer doesn't grant swap; removing the limit makes swap usage unbounded, not zero.
options: --memory 1g --memory-swap 1g — memory-swap is the combined RAM+swap ceiling; equal to memory leaves zero swap
q: A container must use NO swap at all for predictable latency. Which setting?

explain: Process-isolated Windows containers share the host kernel, so image build ≤ host build. Hyper-V isolation virtualizes the kernel and relaxes the match. Newer images are NOT backward compatible with older hosts, and Server hosts are fully supported.
options: Windows containers share the host kernel — with process isolation the image's OS build must be ≤ the host's; use an ltsc2019 image on the 2019 host (or --isolation=hyperv for its own kernel)
q: A servercore ltsc2022 image won't start on a Server 2019 host but runs on 2022. What is the rule?

explain: Mirantis renamed Universal Control Plane → MKE and Docker Trusted Registry → MSR. Old runbooks referencing docker/ucp / docker/dtr are outdated. MKE absolutely still exists, there's no library/ucp namespace move, and MKE installs its own orchestration.
options: Renamed: UCP → MKE, DTR → MSR — install the MKE/MSR images; docker/ucp references are pre-rename and stale
q: A 2019 runbook installs 'Docker UCP' via docker/ucp; the image doesn't exist in 2024. What happened?

explain: True. builder prune is the scoped tool: --filter and --keep-storage give further control. image prune touches images, not build cache; build cache isn't stored as volumes; restarts don't clear it.
q: True or false: docker builder prune reclaims ONLY the BuildKit cache, leaving images, containers, networks, and volumes alone.

explain: bip (bridge IP) re-addresses docker0; fixed-cidr bounds container IPs within it. --ip needs a user-defined network with a matching subnet — and doesn't move docker0 — and Docker's range is movable, which is the point of bip. Network prune doesn't renumber anything.
options: Set bip to 10.200.0.1/24 (with a matching fixed-cidr) in daemon.json and restart — bip defines docker0's address, moving it off the conflicting range
q: docker0's 172.17.0.0/16 collides with the corporate VPN subnet. What fixes the conflict?

explain: True. Binding <1024 requires CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE in the host user namespace, which the unprivileged rootless user lacks — the same rule as item 440. Publishing works fine above 1024, and --network host is disallowed in rootless mode rather than being a fix.
q: True or false: Rootless daemons can't bind ports below 1024 (no CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE) — serve on a high port or lower ip_unprivileged_port_start.

explain: MSR replicas are stateless only when the image store is shared — local-disk storage is per-replica by default. Raft replicates MSR's metadata DB, not blob storage, and rsync between live replicas races with writes.
options: Enable Raft replication for the backend
Configure a shared storage backend (NFS, S3, or another supported object store) in MSR settings so all replicas read/write the same image store
q: MSR replicas with local-disk storage 404 each other's pushes. What makes storage consistent?

explain: Under systemd the daemon's environment comes from unit files, not your shell — hence the drop-in. daemon.json has no proxy keys (a long-standing gap), there is no --proxy pull flag, and hand-launched dockerd is the only case where shell exports would apply.
options: The daemon reads shell http_proxy — export it
The daemon doesn't inherit shell env under systemd — add a drop-in (/etc/systemd/system/docker.service.d/http-proxy.conf with Environment=HTTP_PROXY=...), daemon-reload, restart docker
q: curl works through the proxy but docker pull times out. Why doesn't the daemon see the proxy — where is it set?

explain: --gpus is a frontend for a registered runtime; without the toolkit's runtimes entry the name doesn't resolve. Privileged doesn't create a runtime, --gpus works fine on single hosts, and --device bypasses the runtime model the question is about.
options: The NVIDIA runtime isn't registered — install nvidia-container-toolkit (it registers the nvidia runtime in daemon.json runtimes) and restart the daemon; --gpus maps to that runtime
q: docker run --gpus all fails 'unknown or invalid runtime name: nvidia' on GPU hosts. What's missing?

explain: True. Swarm has two planes: control (always mTLS) and data (VXLAN, plaintext by default). --opt encrypted enables IPsec ESP for the data path at network CREATE time — the same create-time rule as item 651.
q: True or false: Swarm mTLS covers only the control plane; overlay data traffic needs --opt encrypted (IPsec) at network creation.

explain: True. docker_gwbridge is a plain bridge network that can be removed and recreated with a chosen subnet (when no overlay traffic is flowing) — the same procedure as item 453. bip addresses docker0, not gwbridge, and there is no network update command.
q: True or false: docker_gwbridge's subnet is changed by removing and recreating it with the same name and bridge options.

explain: Swarm-scoped networks can't carry node-specific options (parent interfaces differ per host), so the config-only + config-from pattern separates local config from swarm scope. Scope can't be flipped on a local network directly, and promiscuous mode is a NIC setting, not a distribution mechanism.
options: An identical --config-only macvlan network on every node, then one --scope swarm network with --config-from referencing it — services attach to the swarm network; each node applies its local config
q: Swarm doesn't recognize a node-local macvlan network for services. Supported pattern?

explain: ipvlan L3 makes the host act as a router for container subnets with a single MAC — no promiscuous mode, no bridge learning. macvlan always needs promiscuous mode (distinct MACs per container), overlay encryption is unrelated to routability, and L2 is the bridged mode.
options: ipvlan l3 mode (-o ipvlan_mode=l3) — containers share the parent's MAC, the host routes their subnets, no promiscuous mode, IPs directly routable
q: Promiscuous mode is forbidden (no macvlan), but containers need directly-routable IPs, no NAT. Driver and mode?

explain: Ingress mode goes through IPVS + SNAT (node IP seen); host mode binds the published port on the task's node directly — no SNAT. An external LB in front still receives mesh-SNATed traffic from the nodes, and host networking is a different (stronger) change than publish mode.
options: --publish mode=host,target=80 — bypasses the mesh and binds on task nodes directly, preserving the client IP (trade-off: the port exists only where tasks run)
An external LB restores the client IP
q: Behind the mesh, audit logs show node IPs instead of client IPs (SNAT). Keep scheduling, preserve source IPs — how?

explain: tasks.<service> is the documented per-task DNS name on overlay networks, independent of endpoint mode. The .swarm suffix is invented, the VIP is a single virtual IP that never expands, and API scraping is the manual fallback the DNS name exists to avoid.
options: dig +short on the VIP round-robins tasks
tasks.db — the embedded DNS serves A records for each task IP under tasks.<service>, in both VIP and dnsrr modes
q: Config pushes need EVERY task IP of service db, not the VIP. Which DNS name returns them all?

explain: True. Embedded DNS is a user-defined-network feature; the legacy default bridge predates it — the same finding as item 552. --dns sets UPSTREAM resolvers, not name records, and links are the legacy workaround, not the modern default.
q: True or false: The default bridge has no embedded DNS; name resolution (127.0.0.11) exists only on user-defined networks.

explain: True. --internal drops the gateway route — containers talk to each other but can't leave the network. Publishing controls INGRESS, not egress; icc=false blocks container-to-container traffic, the opposite direction; the default bridge has full egress by design.
q: True or false: --internal enforces no internet route for a database tier while peer traffic keeps working.

explain: enable_icc=false programs iptables to drop bridge-forwarded container-to-container packets; the gateway path (external) is untouched — the per-network form of item 464's setting. --internal kills external too, and NetworkPolicy is a Kubernetes construct.
options: -o com.docker.network.bridge.enable_icc=false — disables inter-container communication on the bridge while external connectivity remains
q: Two untrusted workloads share one bridge; direct peer traffic is forbidden, egress must stay. Network-level control?

explain: SCTP support exists in Swarm overlay networking — the long --publish syntax takes protocol=sctp (short syntax: -p 3868:3868/sctp). mode is ingress/host, not a protocol, and protocol=all doesn't exist.
options: --publish published=3868,target=3868,protocol=sctp — Swarm overlays support SCTP publishing; protocol accepts tcp, udp, or sctp
q: A Diameter service needs SCTP 3868. Is host networking really required — what's the Swarm-native option?

explain: True. Enabling the flag without an address pool gives the daemon nowhere to allocate from. fixed-cidr-v6 (daemon) or --ipv6 --subnet (per network) provides the range; single engines do IPv6 fine, and --ipv6 is a network/daemon flag, not a run flag.
q: True or false: daemon.json ipv6: true alone assigns no addresses — a fixed-cidr-v6 pool (or per-network --ipv6 --subnet) is also required.

explain: The embedded DNS at 127.0.0.11 answers for Docker names and forwards everything else to the daemon's configured upstreams (item 352's resolver). Overwriting resolv.conf removes Docker from the path. --dns-search affects suffix expansion, not which server answers.
options: 127.0.0.11 is Docker's embedded DNS — it resolves service/container names and forwards the rest upstream; replacing it bypasses Docker name resolution. Add upstreams via --dns instead
Service names resolve over TCP only
q: resolv.conf was overwritten with the corporate nameserver; service names now fail, external names work. What broke?

explain: Hairpinning (container → host IP:published → back into the container) isn't a supported path; DNAT rules don't cover it. Republishing mode=host changes external behavior without fixing the loop, and the failure is architectural, not a firewall gap.
options: Hairpin NAT — reaching your own published port via the host IP from inside is unreliable; connect via the service DNS name or the container port directly
q: From inside, curl to the host IP's published port times out; external clients are fine. What pattern to avoid?

explain: True. --network container:<name> puts both containers in one net namespace — localhost is literally shared (the same mechanism as item 254's sidecar). Links are legacy and never shared localhost; a published port via the host IP is a different path with NAT in between.
q: True or false: --network container:app makes a sidecar share the app's loopback exactly — the way to scrape a loopback-only app.

explain: default-address-pool defines the bases Docker carves auto-allocated subnets from; it must be set consistently before the swarm is initialized. swarm init takes no --subnet, Docker does not auto-avoid in-use subnets, and per-network --subnet doesn't govern future automatic allocations.
options: default-address-pool in daemon.json (base 10.200.0.0/16, size 24) on every node before swarm init — the pool feeds automatic subnet allocation
q: Auto-created overlays keep colliding with the corporate WAN. Set the fleet-wide allocation pool — where?

explain: True. The ingress network is special-purpose but not special-kind — remove and recreate it with the desired subnet (the same procedure as item 259). No subnet update exists, and rejoining nodes regenerates nothing about ingress.
q: True or false: The ingress subnet is changed by removing and recreating the ingress network with --ingress and the new subnet.

explain: True. --data-path-port exists precisely for VXLAN port conflicts; it must match on all nodes (the same knob as item 546). Published ports are unrelated to the VXLAN underlay, and encryption wraps the payload without changing the UDP port.
q: True or false: A VXLAN port conflict is solved with swarm init --data-path-port 5789, matched on every node.

explain: The number-one config/secret mix-up: different default mount paths. Secrets → /run/secrets/<name> (tmpfs); configs → /<name>. --config works at create time, the file demonstrably exists, and configs aren't encrypted in the container.
options: Configs default to /<config-name> at the container root (secrets default to /run/secrets/<name>) — read /app.conf, or set an explicit target=
q: A config attached as app.conf isn't at /run/secrets/app.conf; exec shows it at /app.conf. Why?

explain: False. Swarm secrets are immutable — there is deliberately no update path. Rotation = new object + --secret-rm/--secret-add in one service update (target= keeps the in-container path stable); the tmpfs is read-only, inline values aren't accepted, and the service need not be recreated.
q: True or false: docker secret update rotates a secret in place without touching the service.

explain: The long --secret syntax carries uid=, gid=, mode= — least privilege at mount time. The mount is read-only (chmod fails), secrets live in the Raft store rather than host files, and configs have the same default-world-readable issue.
options: --secret source=tls.key,target=tls.key,uid=1000,gid=1000,mode=0400 — per-secret uid/gid/mode are set at attach time (writable bit always ignored)
Secrets can't restrict reads; use a config
q: Secrets mount 0444 by default; a TLS key must be readable ONLY by uid 1000. How is it tightened?

explain: MKE's default roles escalate None → View Only → Restricted Control → Scheduler → Full Control. Scheduler deploys/manages services without node/cluster admin — the same least-privilege answer as items 316/701. View Only can't create anything.
options: Replace the grant with Scheduler on /Production — a grant binds subject + role + collection; Scheduler is the deploy-services role, Full Control is cluster-admin
Roles are advisory; only Full Control deploys
q: A deploy bot holds Full Control 'to make CI work'; it only manages services. Least-privilege role, applied how?

explain: Service accounts are non-human identities with their own client bundles — immune to offboarding. Shared admin credentials are an audit nightmare, client bundles DO expire (and embed personal identity), and interactive LDAP logins are unusable for pipelines.
options: Embed a client bundle in the repo
A dedicated MKE service account with Scheduler on the target collection(s) and its own client bundle for CI — not tied to a human's employment
q: CI deploys with a departed admin's personal account; it gets deactivated and pipelines break. Durable pattern?

explain: True. no-new-privileges is the precise control: exec'd binaries can't gain privileges beyond the calling process. Capability drops don't clear setuid bits, read-only doesn't ignore setuid, and non-root users CAN execute setuid-root binaries — that's what setuid means.
q: True or false: --security-opt no-new-privileges neutralizes setuid escalation without dropping capabilities or changing users.

explain: Seccomp is the syscall filter: a custom profile adds back only what's needed instead of removing all filtering. unconfined disables the filter entirely (works, but abandons the protection), capabilities do NOT override seccomp, and AppArmor manages paths/capabilities, not syscalls.
options: A custom seccomp profile (--security-opt seccomp=/etc/docker/agent-profile.json) allowing just the needed syscalls — default-deny kept for everything else
q: A monitoring agent needs a seccomp-blocked syscall; --privileged is on the table. Precise alternative?

explain: User-namespace remapping shifts the container's entire UID range (root → e.g. host uid 100000). --user 0:0 IS host root — the problem, not the fix; userns_mode: host DISABLES remapping (the opposite); SELinux labels confine but don't remap UIDs.
options: --userns-remap default on the daemon — container UIDs (incl. root) map to subordinate host UIDs from /etc/subuid//etc/subgid, so container-root is unprivileged on the host
q: Container-root writes appear as host-root-owned files. Map container-root to an unprivileged host user — how?

explain: False. :ro stops the container replacing the socket FILE; the API behind it has no read-only mode — socket access is full control, equivalent to host root. That's precisely the danger.
q: True or false: A :ro socket mount makes Docker API access from a container read-only and safe.

explain: True. base64 is ENCODING, not encryption — anyone can decode it. Credential helpers delegate to the OS keychain (the credsStore mechanism of item 327). Permissions help, but the secret remains recoverable by anyone who reads the file.
q: True or false: The auth blob in config.json is base64 encoding, not encryption — real protection is a credsStore credential helper.

explain: --read-only + --tmpfs is the standard hardened pattern: immutable image layers, ephemeral writable scratch — the same pairing as item 275. A volume on /tmp doesn't un-read-only the rootfs, and chmod games in the image are build-time state, not a mount policy.
options: docker run --read-only --tmpfs /tmp --tmpfs /run — immutable root filesystem, tmpfs mounts provide writable scratch that never persists
q: Immutable root filesystem required, but the app writes /tmp and a /run PID file. Both requirements hold — how?

explain: Swarm manages its PKI: rotation swaps the CA and reissues node certs automatically (the same operation as item 273's recovery) — no rejoin, no workload impact. Node certs DO expire and rotate; Raft logs are a separate concern.
options: The CA is replaced and node certificates are automatically reissued against it — workloads unaffected; existing certs otherwise expire on schedule
q: An admin runs docker swarm ca --rotate. What actually happens to the cluster?

explain: The daemon API is root-equivalent; --tlsverify enforces mutual TLS so only holders of client certs can connect. 'Private network' is not authentication, port numbers enable nothing by themselves, and docker login authenticates registries, not the daemon API.
options: A docker login password authenticates the API
Mutual TLS: --tlsverify with CA/server certs (port 2376 by convention) and DOCKER_TLS_VERIFY=1 on clients — never expose the unauthenticated API to a network
q: A daemon API exposed on plain-HTTP 2375 is controllable by anyone on the network. Correct way to expose it?

explain: TUF's roles split duties: timestamp = freshness (short-lived, defeats freeze/replay), snapshot = consistency, targets = integrity, root = trust anchor. Root is the LONG-lived anchor — the opposite of the freshness role — and digest pinning is a client habit, not a metadata defense.
options: The timestamp role — timestamp metadata carries a short expiry, so clients reject stale/replayed metadata even when signatures are valid
q: An attacker replays last month's signed metadata to hide a patch (freeze attack). Which DCT/Notary role defeats it?

explain: USER sets the runtime UID; --user overrides it per invocation. setuid goes the WRONG direction (gains privilege), user namespaces aren't on by default so container root is a real escalation concern, and --privileged=false merely declines privileged mode without changing the user.
options: RUN useradd -r appuser and USER appuser before CMD — the process runs unprivileged; operators can still override per-run with docker run --user
q: A scanner flags an image running as root (Dockerfile ends in CMD). Standard fix — and can operators override?

explain: True. AppArmor confines file/network/capability access by path; profiles live on the HOST and are referenced by name. Seccomp filters syscalls, not paths — the LSM roles are the reverse of option-thinking — and capabilities gate operations, not path reads.
q: True or false: Path-level file confinement is AppArmor's job — custom profile on the host, selected with --security-opt apparmor=.

explain: Named-volume initialization copies the image's directory content into a fresh volume — one-time, at first mount (item 396's mechanism). Bind mounts map the host path verbatim. It is engine behavior, not a Postgres quirk, and no other container seeded the volume.
options: Binds populate; named volumes never do
Docker populates a NEW named volume with the image's content at the mount point — bind mounts never populate (the host directory wins as-is)
q: A fresh named volume arrives pre-filled with the image's DB files; a bind mount stays empty. Difference?

explain: False. Bind propagation controls whether submounts propagate: rshared (both ways), rslave (host→container), rprivate (default, none) — the mechanism of item 287. Privileged doesn't change propagation, restarts only re-evaluate once, and :ro is about writes, not mount events.
q: True or false: A container sees later host submounts under a bind automatically; propagation settings are irrelevant.

explain: The local driver accepts type=/o=/device= mount options — an NFS-backed volume with the same name on each node gives every task the same filesystem. Binds require the path on each node and aren't shared by Swarm; named volumes never replicate on their own.
options: docker volume create -d local --opt type=nfs --opt o=addr=10.0.0.5,rw --opt device=:/exports/app appdata on every node, then --mount src=appdata — the same export everywhere
q: A service needs a shared read-write filesystem across nodes; named volumes are node-local. Portable recipe?

explain: True. type=tmpfs with tmpfs-size (bytes) and optional tmpfs-mode gives per-task RAM disks — --mount type=tmpfs IS the service form (--tmpfs is the run shorthand). Named volumes are disk-backed, and there is no tmpfs storage driver.

q: ARG API_KEY is set at build; the RUNNING container's $API_KEY is empty. Why?

explain: True. dockerd --validate is the Docker-aware config check: it catches unknown keys and bad values, not just JSON syntax — python -m json.tool catches syntax only. docker config validate doesn't exist.
q: True or false: dockerd --validate checks daemon.json against the daemon's schema WITHOUT starting the daemon.

explain: True. Volumes are excluded from system prune by default; --volumes opts in (items 342/591's guard). The guard exists because volume data is often irreplaceable; -a absolutely removes unused images.
q: True or false: docker system prune never removes volumes unless --volumes is passed — a deliberate data-safety guard.

explain: True. DOCKER_BUILDKIT=0 falls back to the classic builder per-invocation; the classic builder still ships. The syntax directive only matters to BuildKit, and buildx IS BuildKit.
q: True or false: DOCKER_BUILDKIT=0 docker build selects the classic builder for that one invocation.

explain: True. Rootless Docker delegates subordinate UID/GID setup to the setuid newuidmap/newgidmap binaries from the uidmap package — the specific missing piece the error names. A kernel gap would fail differently; no reboot or root is needed.
q: True or false: Rootless dockerd failing 'newuidmap not found' means the uidmap package (newuidmap/newgidmap) is missing.

explain: Container DNS is explicit: --dns (per container) or daemon.json "dns" (default for all) — the container's resolv.conf is built from these, independent of the host's resolver. In-container resolv.conf edits are ephemeral; DNS is never set in the Dockerfile.
options: Per container with --dns 10.0.0.2, or daemon-wide with "dns": ["10.0.0.2"] in daemon.json — container resolv.conf is built from these, independent of the host's resolver
Set the nameserver in the Dockerfile
q: Containers must resolve corporate names via 10.0.0.2; the host uses a public resolver. Where is container DNS set?

explain: True. -p [IP:]hostport:containerport — omitting the IP binds all interfaces (0.0.0.0); 127.0.0.1 scopes it to loopback. Docker binds selectively just fine, and host networking exposes MORE, not less.
q: True or false: -p 127.0.0.1:8080:80 binds the published port to localhost only — the IP field scopes the bind.

explain: True. IPv6 is configured on the daemon ("ipv6": true + fixed-cidr-v6) and per network — the flag the engineer reached for doesn't exist (item 756's rule). Docker routes IPv6 fine once enabled.
q: True or false: There is no per-container --ipv6 flag — IPv6 is a daemon-level setting (ipv6 + fixed-cidr-v6 in daemon.json).

explain: --network-alias registers a name on ONE network's DNS; repeat per network for different names (items 310/576/696's mechanism). A container has exactly one hostname, and aliases work on plain user-defined networks, not just Swarm.
options: --network-alias web on frontend and --network-alias api-internal on backend — aliases are per-network, unlike the single container-wide hostname
q: One container must answer as 'web' on frontend and 'api-internal' on backend. How?

explain: --default-addr-pool reserves the CIDR space Swarm carves overlay subnets from, and it's init-time-only (items 768/546's pool). No swarm update path exists; data-path-port is the VXLAN data port, unrelated to addressing.
options: Change it anytime via swarm update
Init with --default-addr-pool 10.20.0.0/16 (plus --default-addr-pool-mask-length as needed) — the pool is fixed AT INIT; changing it later means leaving and re-initializing the swarm
q: Corporate LAN already uses 10.0.0.0/8; Swarm's default overlay pool would collide. How is it avoided?

explain: True. pids-limit is the cgroup pids controller applied per container — the direct fork-bomb defense. Memory limits don't bound task counts, and CPU limits don't cap process numbers.
q: True or false: --pids-limit 256 caps a container's processes/threads in its cgroup — the control that contains a fork bomb.

explain: Drop-all-then-add is the least-privilege pattern (item 302's allowlist); enumerating drops is fragile against future defaults. --privileged=false just means 'not privileged' — the default cap set still applies; verify via CapDrop/CapAdd in docker inspect.
options: --cap-drop ALL, then --cap-add only what's needed (e.g. CHOWN) — deny by default, grant the minimal set
q: Compliance demands the absolute minimum capabilities (default grants ~14). Correct pattern?

explain: True. Docker Bench is an audit script, not a remediation tool — it reports pass/warn/notes against the CIS Docker Benchmark and changes nothing itself. The CIS Docker Benchmark very much exists, and Bench applies to any Docker host.
q: True or false: Docker Bench for Security CHECKS config against the CIS benchmark and reports — it remediates nothing itself.

explain: Dropping root via USER/--user is baseline hardening; the classic follow-on bug is volume permission denials for the non-root UID. Root-in-container is still high-risk (kernel exploits, capability abuse), and USER needs no --privileged.
options: Add USER app (creating the user in the image) or --user on run/service create — and ensure that user has permissions on mounted volumes, or writes fail
Root in a container is harmless (namespaces)
q: A scan flags all-root containers (image has no USER). Fix, and what must be watched?

explain: True. SELinux decisions use labels: Docker sets them on volume content it manages, but never relabels arbitrary host paths unasked — hence :z/:Z (items 262/513's mechanism). Volumes are labeled, not exempt, and bind mounts work fine with SELinux once labeled.
q: True or false: Bind mounts keep host SELinux labels (denied without :z/:Z); Docker auto-labels named-volume content — hence the difference.

explain: The documented pattern is a transient container with the volume plus a host bind for the archive (items 399/484's approach). No docker volume export command exists, and copying the raw volume dir under a live daemon risks inconsistent data.
options: docker run --rm -v data:/data -v $(pwd):/backup busybox tar czf /backup/data.tar.gz -C / data — a throwaway container holding both mounts does the copy; no volume export command exists
Named volumes can't be backed up
q: Back up a named volume's data into a host tarball. How?

explain: True. The built-in local driver accepts type=nfs with mount options — the plugin-free NFS path. Bind mounts are strictly local paths, and there is no driver literally named 'nfs'.
q: True or false: docker volume create -d local with --opt type=nfs mounts NFS with no third-party plugin.

explain: rprivate means mount/unmount events don't propagate into the container; rshared/rslave opt into propagation (items 287/786's mechanism). Recreating works but misses the mechanism; --privileged is not the fix.
options: Propagation defaults to rprivate — the container's namespace doesn't receive host submounts; use shared propagation (-v /mnt/data:/data:rshared, host side shared too)
q: The host mounts a new disk under a bind-mounted path; the container never sees it. Why, and the fix?

explain: True. Autolock encrypts Raft logs/TLS keys at rest; after a daemon restart the manager needs the unlock key via docker swarm unlock. Re-init would DESTROY the swarm, and the lock persists across restarts by design.
q: True or false: With --autolock, a rebooted manager stays locked ('Swarm is encrypted') until docker swarm unlock with the unlock key.

explain: True. Quorum = floor(n/2)+1: for n=2 that's 2, so ANY single loss halts the control plane. Run 3 or 5 managers (odd): 3 tolerates 1 failure, 5 tolerates 2 — even counts add nodes without adding fault tolerance.
q: True or false: A 2-manager swarm loses quorum when one dies (quorum is 2) — run 3 or 5 managers instead.

explain: True. drain = evict + reschedule + no-new-tasks (maintenance); pause = freeze scheduling only, existing tasks keep running (diagnostics). The two states are distinct, and removing the node is overkill for maintenance.
q: True or false: For maintenance use node availability drain (evicts tasks); pause only stops NEW placements, tasks keep running.

explain: True. Global mode honors constraints: one task per matching node, self-maintaining as workers join (item 711's pattern). A fixed replica count rots on every cluster change, and unconstrained global hits managers too.
q: True or false: --mode global --constraint 'node.role==worker' runs the agent on every worker, never on managers, incl. future workers.

domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry
explain: False. Two pushes to one tag OVERWRITE each other. A manifest list is assembled explicitly — docker manifest create --amend per arch, then manifest push (or buildx --platform in one step).
q: True or false: Pushing per-arch images to the same tag makes the registry merge them into a manifest list.

domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry
explain: imagetools inspect resolves the tag remotely and prints the manifest list — the authoritative answer. docker inspect shows only the LOCAL platform's manifest; pulling per-arch is toil that proves nothing about the list.
options: Pull the tag on each architecture
The registry UI always shows platforms
docker buildx imagetools inspect registry.corp/app:v2 — reads the manifest list from the registry: platforms, per-arch digests, attestations
q: After pushing a multi-arch image, verify which platforms the tag serves. How?

domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry
explain: --chown/--chmod on COPY avoids the duplicate-layer rewrite that RUN chown causes — the files exist twice across layers (items 119/218's waste pattern). ADD doesn't set ownership, and ownership matters for runtime permissions.
options: chown needs its own layer — already optimal
COPY --chown=app:app --chmod=755 . /app — ownership/mode set AT COPY time: no extra layer, smaller image, better caching
q: COPY . then RUN chown -R bloats the image and slows rebuilds. Better pattern?

domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry
explain: True. Hub throttles anonymous pulls hardest; authenticating raises the quota substantially — the standard CI fix, plus a mirror/pull-through cache for scale. The limit is per-account/IP, not per image name, and it applies to pulls exactly as the error says.
q: True or false: 'toomanyrequests' pull limits are fixed by authenticating (docker login) — anonymous pulls get the lowest quota.

explain: Proxy env for the daemon needs NO_PROXY exceptions for internal hosts — the classic 'proxy broke internal pulls' fix. Removing the proxy sacrifices internet pulls; insecure-registries governs TLS policy, not proxy routing.
options: Add the internal addresses to NO_PROXY in the dockerd systemd proxy drop-in (NO_PROXY=10.20.0.5,10.0.0.0/8), daemon-reload + restart — without exceptions, even internal pulls route to the proxy
Internal registries can't coexist with a proxy
q: Daemon proxy set; pulls from the INTERNAL registry (10.20.0.5:5000) now route to the egress proxy and fail. Fix?

explain: True. Docker defaults to HTTPS for registries; opting out is a daemon-level insecure-registries entry — no per-pull insecure flag exists (the classic invented-flag trap).
q: True or false: Plain-HTTP registries are enabled via daemon.json insecure-registries + restart — there is no docker pull --insecure flag.

explain: True. --gpus is the supported interface (all, or device IDs); the toolkit handles device nodes, libraries, and driver wiring — verify with nvidia-smi inside. Installation alone attaches nothing, and --privileged is the overkill myth.
q: True or false: GPU access is granted with docker run --gpus all (nvidia-container-toolkit installed) — not --privileged.

explain: The daemon (usually started by systemd with its own LimitNOFILE) seeds container ulimits — your interactive shell limits are irrelevant. Set --ulimit nofile=65536:65536 per container or default-ulimits in daemon.json.
options: Containers receive the DAEMON's default ulimits, not your shell's — set --ulimit nofile=65536:65536 on run/service create, or default-ulimits in daemon.json
q: 'Too many open files' inside containers; the host's limits are high. Why?

explain: mode=host|vip|ingress is a long-syntax-only field on service publish (items 259/767's syntax). The short form can't express it; --network host discards Swarm networking entirely rather than publishing one port in host mode.
options: Host-mode publishing is impossible for services
Long publish syntax: --publish published=8080,target=80,protocol=tcp,mode=host — the mode field exists only in the long form
q: A service port must publish in HOST mode (bypass ingress mesh, keep client IPs). Short -p can't express it. How?

explain: True. --internal drops the gateway/egress path but leaves container-to-container traffic working. Publishing controls INGRESS only; icc=false blocks the container traffic the requirement needs.
q: True or false: docker network create --internal gives app↔database traffic with NO internet route — egress is dropped, ICC stays.

explain: True. Prune is safe by default: only networks with no endpoints are removed. In-use networks are protected, and volumes are a separate prune entirely.
q: True or false: docker network prune removes only UNUSED networks — any network with connected endpoints is left alone.

explain: True. ICC=false cuts container-to-container traffic on the bridge; ingress via published ports is unaffected (items 464/760's control). --link is a legacy name mechanism, not an isolation control.
q: True or false: --icc=false (or the bridge enable_icc opt) isolates containers on a bridge while published ports keep working.

explain: Build-args leak via docker history/metadata; BuildKit secret mounts exist precisely for build-time credentials (item 86's fix). ENV is WORSE — baked into the runtime environment; build-time secrets are entirely possible, just not via ARG.
options: --build-arg values persist in image history/metadata — use RUN --mount=type=secret,id=feedtoken with docker build --secret id=feedtoken,src=./token.txt: mounted only for that RUN step, never committed to a layer
ENV is more secure than ARG
q: A build token passed via --build-arg must not land in any layer. What's wrong, and the fix?

explain: False. Existing signatures verify with the PUBLIC key, which stays published. What the lost private key blocks is NEW signed tags — recovery is rotating to a new key/delegation; private keys can't be regenerated identically.
q: True or false: Losing a DCT signing private key makes previously signed tags unverifiable.

explain: MKE delegates auth to the IdP via SAML/LDAP and applies its own RBAC to the asserted identity — MFA lives at the IdP. SAML never gives MKE the password, and MFA can't be enforced in local user settings for federated users.
options: Point MKE's SAML backend at the IdP — authentication incl. MFA is delegated; MKE maps the asserted identity to users/teams for RBAC
Enforce MFA in MKE's local settings
q: Policy mandates MFA via the corporate SAML IdP for all admin access. How does MKE integrate?

explain: True. Digests stop tag-mutation attacks; signatures stop publisher-impersonation attacks. Dropping either leaves a hole — DCT is not deprecated, and digests are stable by design.
q: True or false: Digest pinning (WHAT bits) and DCT signing (WHO published) defend different attacks — pinning doesn't make signing redundant.

explain: True. Anonymous volumes are recreated per container and orphaned on replace — the classic compose disk leak. Only docker rm -v removes them with the container; the fix is named volumes plus volume prune for the orphans.
q: True or false: Dozens of random-hex volumes mean anonymous volumes in compose; fix with named volumes + prune.

explain: size= is backend-dependent: devicemapper natively, overlay2/zfs only with quota-capable backing filesystems. tmpfs-size caps only tmpfs mounts, not the writable layer.
options: --storage-opt size=10G — but only on supporting backends (devicemapper, or overlay2/zfs on quota-capable filesystems like XFS pquota); check driver/filesystem first
q: A runaway writer fills the shared disk. Per-container disk cap — what works?

explain: False. Seeding happens only for fresh NAMED volumes (copied from the image once, when empty). A bind mount simply overlays the host directory as-is — empty stays empty.
q: True or false: A bind mount to an empty host directory is seeded with the image's content, like a named volume.

explain: local-persist pins a named volume to a chosen host path — volume semantics with a fixed location. Symlinks under the daemon's directory are fragile and unsupported; moving all of /var/lib/docker for one path requirement is disproportionate.
options: Replace named volumes with bind mounts
The local-persist plugin — maps named volumes to deterministic host paths (volume create -d local-persist -o mountpoint=/data/volumes/<name>); still node-local, just addressable
q: Named volumes must live at predictable paths under /data/volumes/<name> for a restricted backup agent. What provides this?

explain: True. vfs = naive full copies, no CoW, no sharing between layers — correct but the slowest, most wasteful driver; a fallback/debugging driver, not for production. Swarm doesn't require it, and driver choice directly drives disk usage.
q: True or false: vfs copies the full filesystem per layer (no copy-on-write) — a fallback driver; production belongs on overlay2.

explain: True. include (Compose 2.20+) is the composition mechanism: it pulls whole additional Compose files — local paths or remote URLs — into the current project. extends is the reuse mechanism: it copies/merges one SERVICE's fields into another within files Compose can already read.
q: True or false: include: merges whole Compose files (even remote URLs) into a project; extends: reuses individual service definitions.

explain: True. Watch rules are per-path actions: sync streams file changes into the running container (fast, no rebuild), rebuild rebuilds the image when dependencies change, restart just restarts. Watch is a Compose feature, not stack deploy, and sync needs no SSH daemon.
q: True or false: compose watch 'sync' copies files into the running container with no rebuild; 'rebuild' rebuilds — they differ by design.

explain: Profiles are opt-in groups: any service with a profiles: list is skipped unless one of its profiles is enabled via --profile or COMPOSE_PROFILES (item 835's rule). There is no --force-profiles flag, and profiles are ignored by — not exclusive to — stack deploy.
options: docker compose --profile debug up -d — profiled services are excluded by default and start only when their profile is enabled (COMPOSE_PROFILES=debug works too)
Profiles only affect stack deploy — restart the daemon
A profiled service can never start via up
q: debug-tools carries profiles: ['debug'] and didn't start on compose up. Start it now, no file edits — how?

explain: True. Swarm does not honor depends_on (short or long syntax) — one of the Compose keys the stack deploy path ignores, along with build, container_name, and restart (items 314/830's rule). Ordering guarantees simply don't exist in Swarm; the service must retry.
q: True or false: After stack deploy, depends_on condition: service_healthy is ignored — Swarm schedules all services independently.

explain: False. Buildx never pushes unless told: --push on the CLI or push = true in the bake target — and plain buildx build doesn't push either. Bake's default group builds all targets, honoring their outputs.
q: True or false: buildx bake pushes every target automatically once the build succeeds.

explain: True. Bake's --set flag overrides any target attribute at invocation time (--set <target>.<field>=<value>, with * as a wildcard target) — the designed mechanism for CI parameterization without file edits. Build args override build args, not target fields.
q: True or false: A bake target's tag is overridden at invocation with --set api.tags=... — no file edit needed.

explain: --build-arg values are interpolated into the Dockerfile instructions and baked into layer history (docker history shows the full RUN line). BuildKit secret mounts never end up in any layer (items 86/892's fix). ENV is worse — baked into the runtime environment — and secret mounts work with both build drivers.
options: Secret mounts need the docker driver only
Pass --secret id=token,src=... in the CI invocation too — the --build-arg expands the token into a RUN layer, visible in docker history and image config forever; secret mounts never land in any layer
ENV TOKEN in the Dockerfile — env vars are stripped at push
build-args are safe; ARG never persists
q: CI fails 'secret not found' for --mount=type=secret; a teammate proposes --build-arg TOKEN=$(cat token.txt). Why is that dangerous, and the correct fix?
