explain: Precedence: credHelpers (per-registry) beats credsStore (global default) — this registry's credential goes to pass; every other registry falls back to the macOS keychain (item 809's helper system, resolved). docker login writes to auths only when no store/helper applies.
options: The macOS keychain — credsStore always wins
Base64 in config.json auths — login always writes auths
The pass helper — a per-registry credHelpers entry takes precedence over the global credsStore for that registry
q: config.json has credsStore: osxkeychain AND credHelpers for registry.internal.example → pass. Where does that registry's login credential go?

explain: True. The Docker CLI resolves the daemon endpoint with clear precedence: DOCKER_HOST (and friends like DOCKER_TLS_VERIFY) override whatever context is active (item 813's rule). The asterisk shows which context WOULD be used if the variable were unset.
q: True or false: DOCKER_HOST=ssh://admin@node2 wins over the active context — context ls's '*' shows only the fallback.

explain: True. Live restore bridges DAEMON downtime: the daemon can stop, crash, or upgrade while containerd keeps workloads alive (item 650's scope). A host reboot is outside that contract — the kernel is gone, so everything stops, and restart policies bring containers back.
q: True or false: live-restore covers daemon restarts/upgrades only — a host reboot stops everything; restart policies do the recovery.

explain: User namespaces remap the container's UID 0 to a high, unprivileged host UID (default dockremap:231072:65536 in /etc/subuid) — host-root-owned bind-mount content is suddenly owned by 'someone else' (items 439/776/821's shift). Remap doesn't force the nobody user, needs no :Z, and works fine with bind mounts once ownership is fixed.
options: userns-remap maps container uid 0 to an unprivileged subordinate UID (dockremap range) — host files owned by real root become inaccessible; chown the directory into the mapped range
Remap forces all containers to nobody
Remap is incompatible with bind mounts
q: After enabling userns-remap, a bind-mounted host directory denies writes; files are host-root-owned; the app runs as container root. What changed?

explain: True. The daemon-wide dns list becomes the default upstream resolver for containers (it lands in their resolv.conf / is used by the embedded server as forwarder). The embedded DNS at 127.0.0.11 remains authoritative for container names on user-defined networks.
q: True or false: daemon.json "dns" sets containers' default upstream DNS — it does NOT replace the embedded 127.0.0.11 name resolver.

explain: VIP mode (default) gives one virtual IP with kernel-level (IPVS) load balancing — perfect for clients, useless for per-task scraping. DNSRR mode makes the embedded DNS return every task IP, pushing the iteration to the client (item 772's trade-off). There is no host endpoint mode.
options: --endpoint-mode dnsrr — DNS for the service name returns EVERY task's IP; the scraper iterates them itself; no virtual IP balances anymore
Endpoint mode only affects published ports
q: A scraper must reach EACH task of a service; the service name only ever hits one. Which endpoint mode, and what changes?

explain: False. Ingress binds the port once per node via the routing mesh; host mode binds the port in EACH task's namespace — two tasks on one node collide. Host mode trades the mesh for direct binding.
q: True or false: Two tasks on one node can share a mode=host published port, like ingress mode.

explain: --attachable explicitly opens a Swarm overlay to manually-attached standalone containers (the classic debugging use case, items 257/817's flag). Without it, the network is exclusive to service tasks; overlays work on workers fine, and no alias grants admission.
options: Standalone containers can never join overlays
The overlay needs --attachable — without it, only Swarm-managed tasks may join; standalone docker run containers are rejected
q: docker run --network myoverlay fails: 'network cannot be used' by standalone containers, though services attach fine. What's missing?

explain: False. --internal cuts only the network's EXTERNAL route; intra-network connectivity and DNS stay intact — the app reaches the DB, and a dual-homed proxy can ferry updates while the DB stays isolated.
q: True or false: --internal also blocks container-to-container traffic, so even the app can't reach the database.

explain: True. --aux-address carves named exclusions out of the pool IPAM allocates dynamically — keeping a static IP from colliding with DHCP-style assignment; --ip-range narrows the dynamic slice. Both act at network creation; an aux reservation can't reclaim an address already leased before it existed — which is why a later --ip can still collide with a pre-reservation lease.
q: True or false: --aux-address reserves IPs out of the dynamic pool; --ip-range narrows the dynamic slice.

explain: chown needs CAP_CHOWN; with ALL dropped, even uid 0 is denied — capabilities are enforced against root too once removed from the bounding set (item 869's allowlist, applied). --privileged would restore everything to fix one syscall-class operation; drop-ALL combines with cap-add by design.
options: Remove --cap-drop=ALL — it can't combine with cap-add
Run as root — uid 0 bypasses caps
Add --cap-add=CHOWN — ownership changes need CAP_CHOWN, dropped with ALL; the teammate is wrong: capability checks bind uid 0 too once a cap leaves the bounding set
q: --cap-drop=ALL, only NET_BIND_SERVICE added. Entrypoint chown fails: 'Operation not permitted'. Teammate: 'just run as root.' Minimal fix, and why is he wrong?

explain: True. Even on --read-only containers, Docker mounts /etc/hosts, /etc/hostname, and /etc/resolv.conf as individual writable bind mounts managed by the daemon, living outside the container's rootfs. The flag locks the image layers, not these runtime-managed files.
q: True or false: Under --read-only, /etc/hosts, /etc/hostname, /etc/resolv.conf stay writable — Docker bind-mounts them separately; name resolution keeps working.

explain: --tlsverify means the daemon requires mutually-authenticated TLS: clients must present a cert signed by the daemon's CA (item 846's transport). The CLI gets that material from DOCKER_CERT_PATH (ca.pem, cert.pem, key.pem). The daemon never auto-issues client certs, and 2375 is the plaintext port — the opposite direction.
options: Nothing — the daemon auto-issues client certs
The client must present certificates: DOCKER_TLS_VERIFY=1 + DOCKER_CERT_PATH (or --tlsverify --tlscacert/--tlscert/--tlskey) — without them the daemon rejects the handshake
Use port 2375 — TLS daemons upgrade there
q: DOCKER_HOST=tcp://manager:2376 against a --tlsverify daemon: every command fails the TLS handshake. The daemon is up. What is the client missing?

explain: False. Swarm secrets are capped at 500KB each, compressed or not — they are the encrypted channel (Raft log + transit + tmpfs). The license belongs in a CONFIG: same distribution machinery, unencrypted and uncapped.
q: True or false: A 2MB license file fits in a Swarm secret if it is compressed first.

explain: The local driver's --opt type=nfs --opt o=addr=... --opt device=:/path passes straight through to the kernel mount — NFS, CIFS, tmpfs-style mounts are all fair game with zero plugins (items 874/922's mechanism). Plugins like REX-Ray add provisioning intelligence, not basic NFS.
options: It works on one node only; data isn't shared
Local only manages host directories — plugin required
The engineer — local accepts type/device/o mount options and mounts anything the kernel supports, incl. NFS and CIFS; no plugin needed for basic NFS
q: Local-driver NFS volume works on every node; a teammate insists NFS needs a plugin. Who is right?

explain: This is the documented -v vs --mount divergence: -v is lenient (creates missing host paths as root), --mount is strict (bind sources must pre-exist). The strictness is the safer default — a typo in -v silently creates a wrong, root-owned directory and the app runs against empty data.
options: --mount requires the bind source to exist and fails fast; -v silently creates it as root — --mount's explicitness is safer (auto-created root-owned dirs are a classic permission-bug source)
Both auto-create; it was a target= typo
q: -v auto-created a missing host dir; --mount type=bind failed 'source does not exist'. What behavioral difference is this, and which is safer?

explain: True. tmpfs mounts live in host memory (page cache, swappable under pressure), never in the storage driver, and evaporate with the container (items 788/847/924's mount) — the textbook fit for sensitive ephemeral scratch. Secrets are also tmpfs but are a distribution mechanism, not general scratch space, and tmpfs size= IS honored.
q: True or false: --tmpfs /cache is RAM-backed, container-scoped, and size-cappable.

explain: Prune filters are ANDed with the 'unused' criterion: the command considers only unused volumes, then keeps only those matching the filter — label!=keep matches volumes lacking the label, so the ten labeled volumes are excluded from deletion even if unused (item 591's filter logic). label=keep would delete exactly the protected set.
options: docker volume prune --filter "label!=keep" — prune deletes unused volumes; the filter narrows candidates first: only unused volumes WITHOUT the keep label are removed
prune prompts per volume — answer no 10 times
Labels can't be set on volumes
q: 30 scratch volumes; 10 critical, labeled keep=true. Which single prune command removes the scratch and provably spares the labeled?

explain: False. Autolock encrypts Raft logs at rest and the key exists nowhere in the cluster — a lost key makes that manager's local state unrecoverable. Remove it from a healthy manager, rotate the key, and rejoin it fresh.
q: True or false: A locked manager's unlock key can be recovered from the other managers' Raft state.

explain: True. Join tokens are single-use-at-join credentials: the manager validates the token when a node joins, then issues a mutual-TLS certificate (item 384's rule). After that, membership rides on the certificate, not the token — no grace period, no CA rotation needed.
q: True or false: Rotating a join token affects only NEW joins — existing nodes ride on their issued certificates and are unaffected.

explain: Compose file stacking is last-wins: each additional -c file overrides the merged result of the previous ones, key by key. That's the entire point of the base+override pattern (base.yaml for shared config, prod.yaml for environment specifics). All keys merge this way, not just deploy:.
options: Later files override earlier ones on conflicting keys (same rule as compose -f stacking) — prod.yaml wins; use file order deliberately: base under environment overrides
Conflicting keys are a deploy error
q: stack deploy takes base.yaml then prod.yaml; prod's replicas and logging win. What's the multi-file merge rule?

explain: True. Job modes (replicated-job, global-job) model run-to-completion work: success is terminal, and only non-zero exits are retried (default on-failure restart). Completed tasks linger as records until the task-history limit rolls them off — they are not deleted on success.
q: True or false: replicated-job tasks that exit 0 are done, not restarted; only failures retry.

explain: True. The long secret syntax is fully honored by Swarm: target sets the in-container filename, uid/gid/mode set ownership/permissions (defaults: root-owned, 0444). The short syntax (- tls_key) is where the filename defaults to the source name.
q: True or false: Swarm's long secret syntax honors target/uid/gid/mode — secrets land at /run/secrets/<target>, not always the source name.

domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry
explain: --build-arg performs textual substitution into RUN instructions, and that text is permanently recorded in layer metadata — docker history on any machine with the image reveals it (items 907/931's leak). ENV is visible in docker inspect — worse, not redacted; .dockerignore governs the build context, not history.
options: build-args are stripped; the scanner read the cache

The token is baked into layer history because --build-arg interpolates into the instruction text — anyone with the image reads it via docker history. Safe pattern: BuildKit secret mount (RUN --mount=type=secret + --secret), never in any layer
Switch ARG to ENV — env is redacted from history
q: docker history shows the full Bearer token from a --build-arg TOKEN build. Correct diagnosis and safe pattern?

domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry
explain: Inline cache piggybacks on the image itself: cache metadata is embedded in the image config, so every pull carries it (hence the bloat). Registry cache (type=registry,ref=...) writes cache blobs as separate manifests under the ref — the image stays lean. Registry cache works with any OCI registry, not just Hub.
options: type=inline embeds cache metadata INTO the pushed image config (bloating every image); type=registry stores cache as separate manifests under ref — the image stays lean
Inline is a no-op; registry is the only real backend
q: --cache-to type=inline speeds builds but every image grows ~200MB. A teammate suggests type=registry,ref=app:buildcache. What's the difference?

domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry
explain: False. Mirrors are pull-through caches ONLY; the push path never consults them — pushes go to the canonical upstream registry. Pushing to the mirror's own address writes into the mirror's storage, not upstream.
q: True or false: CI should push nightly builds to the registry mirror so nodes pull them locally.

domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry
explain: False. With -a, prune removes every image not used by at least one EXISTING container (running or stopped, ancestry included). A Compose file on disk creates no reference — only containers protect images.
q: True or false: image prune -a spares images referenced by a stopped Compose project on disk.

explain: Managed plugin configuration (docker plugin set) mutates the plugin's rootfs/env, which is only safe while the plugin is stopped — hence the disabled-required rule (item 545's lifecycle). And disable isn't free: containers using the plugin's volumes depend on it, so quiesce them first.
options: Options are install-time only — reinstall with -e
plugin set works on running plugins; DEBUG is invalid
plugin set only works on DISABLED plugins — that's the failure; and disabling a plugin whose volumes are in use is blocked/unsafe: quiesce dependent containers first, then disable → set → enable
q: docker plugin set vieux/sshfs DEBUG=1 fails: 'plugin must be disabled first'. A teammate warns disabling breaks in-use volumes. Correct lifecycle understanding?

explain: True. MKE (UCP) ships against a validated Engine matrix; the installer preflights the engine version and refuses unsupported ones — newer included (item 988's pin). This is deliberate: the control plane depends on specific Engine behaviors. The remedy is a supported Engine release.
q: True or false: MKE's installer preflight rejects a too-NEW Engine — MKE supports only validated Engine versions; install a supported release.

explain: True. UCP/MKE backup encryption is passphrase-based and the passphrase exists nowhere in the cluster by design — lose it and the backup is cryptographically unrecoverable. Companion facts: store the passphrase in the vault with the backup, test restores, and restores require the SAME MKE version that produced the backup.
q: True or false: An MKE backup's encryption passphrase is stored NOWHERE in the cluster — lose it and the tarball is unrecoverable.

explain: Docker applies a default seccomp profile (blocking ~44 risky syscalls) to every non-privileged container (item 818's profile). The surgical fix is a custom profile: copy the default, allow the one syscall, attach per container. There is no daemon-wide seccomp toggle, and capabilities are a separate mechanism from syscall filtering.
options: A custom seccomp profile JSON allowing just the needed syscall (based on the default), passed per container via --security-opt seccomp=/path/custom.json — the default stays in force everywhere else
q: A legacy binary dies on a mount-family syscall; it works with seccomp=unconfined. Keep the default profile for everything else — right approach?

explain: True. --opt encrypted enables IPsec for the overlay data plane (node-to-node VXLAN). The control plane (manager Raft, gossip) is always mutual-TLS encrypted — never optional. Ingress/published traffic rides the host network outside the overlay, untouched by this flag — and encryption costs CPU.
q: True or false: --opt encrypted encrypts the overlay VXLAN data plane (IPsec) — NOT published-port ingress; control plane was already mTLS.

explain: True. Swarm services are multi-network citizens: each --network adds an attachment with its own VIP and DNS registration, and --network-add/--network-rm mutate attachments on a live service via rolling update. No endpoint-mode condition applies.
q: True or false: A service attaches to MULTIPLE networks (--network frontend --network backend) — one task interface and VIP per network.

explain: False. ipvlan L2 multiplexes many container IPs onto the parent interface's SINGLE MAC — the MAC-table-friendly answer when switches cap entries. macvlan is the one minting per-container MACs (and needing promiscuous mode).
q: True or false: ipvlan L2 mints a unique MAC per container, like macvlan, but routes better.

explain: --link is legacy default-bridge-only machinery: it wrote /etc/hosts entries and injected ALIAS_PORT-style env vars. On user-defined networks Docker provides embedded DNS instead (name resolution by container/service name). --link was deprecated, not removed — containers on the default bridge still honor it.
options: --link only functions on the default bridge — on user-defined networks it's silently ignored, so the injection never happens; replacement: embedded DNS (reach deps by name) + explicit -e for config
User-defined networks block env vars — use --env-file
The vars moved to docker inspect
q: Migrating off --link to a user-defined network, the injected env vars vanish. What changed, and the modern replacement?

explain: The pattern is a purpose-built identity: a service account (local MKE user) + a minimal grant (Scheduler × /Prod/Web) + its own client bundle (items 826/943's model) — least privilege (deploy-only, one collection), attributable, and revocable without touching any human's access. LDAP bind credentials are not MKE API tokens.
options: Share the admin's bundle — pipelines are trusted
The LDAP bind DN doubles as an API token
A dedicated MKE service account granted Scheduler scoped to /Prod/Web, with THAT account's client bundle in the pipeline — deploy rights in one collection, attributable and independently revocable
Bundles can't be scoped — Full Control or nothing
q: CI must deploy to MKE's /Prod/Web collection; the team refuses a human admin's bundle in the pipeline. Least-privilege credentialing?

explain: False. A bundle is per-user: it carries that user's certificates (Swarm + Kubernetes) and embedded permissions. Sharing it lets anyone impersonate the owner with their full access — every user downloads their own.
q: True or false: An MKE client bundle is a cluster-wide read-only credential, safe to share with the team.

explain: True. Swarm runs its own PKI: each node gets a mutual-TLS certificate the swarm automatically reissues on a ~90-day rotation — no operator action, no restarts (item 994's CA, default side). --external-ca at init/join lets an external CA sign instead; ca --rotate is for CA compromise/re-keying, not a daily cron.
q: True or false: Swarm node TLS certs auto-rotate ~every 90 days by default; --external-ca at init/join substitutes the corporate PKI.

explain: True. The daemon --icc flag is default-bridge-only (a legacy control). User-defined bridges expose the same control per network via the com.docker.network.bridge.enable_icc driver option at creation time (items 464/760/891's control, per-network form). --icc is not a docker run flag.
q: True or false: Daemon --icc=false governs only the default bridge — user-defined bridges take --opt com.docker.network.bridge.enable_icc=false at create.

explain: True. docker compose down removes containers and networks; -v/--volumes extends that to named volumes declared in the compose file — the Compose CLI's classic data-loss footgun. Anonymous volumes are also removed by down -v, but named ones are only safe from down WITHOUT -v.
q: True or false: compose down -v removes named volumes declared in the file too.

explain: The helper-container tar pattern is the idiomatic volume backup (items 399/484/873) — the flaw is timing, not tooling. Copying a running DB's data files races its writes; you get a torn, unrecoverable image. --rm removes the helper CONTAINER, not the volume, and docker cp has the same consistency problem.
options: tar can't read mounts — use docker cp
A filesystem copy of a LIVE database is inherently inconsistent (WAL/journal mid-write) — tar faithfully copied a torn state; stop the container (or use the DB's native dump) for a consistent backup
q: Helper-container tar backups of a RUNNING database restore corrupt. The team blames tar. Real problem and correct pattern?

explain: False. Read-only is a property of the MOUNT, not the volume: each container's flags are independent, so the :rw container still writes shared data. Fix lock-file crashes with a tmpfs or separate writable mount.
q: True or false: Marking one container's mount :ro makes the whole volume read-only for every container.

explain: Production devicemapper means direct-lvm: a real block device backing the thin pool (dm.thinpooldev, dm.use_deferred_deletion — items 822/849's fix), because loopback files serialize I/O and risk corruption. Storage options are daemon-level, never per-container, and driver changes never migrate data.
options: Ignore it — loopback is fine on SSD

Direct-lvm: thin pool on the block device + dm.thinpooldev in daemon.json — but changing the backing makes existing /var/lib/docker content inaccessible, so push/save images and back up volumes BEFORE the switch
Switch to overlay2 — it migrates the data
q: docker info warns devicemapper is on loopback; a spare 200GB block device exists. Production-grade fix, and what happens to existing data?

explain: True. Update supervision works in three parts: monitor is how long each updated task is watched before it's considered successful; max_failure_ratio is the tolerated fraction of failures; failure_action decides what happens when the ratio is breached. 3/10 = 30% > 0.2, so rollback fires. rollback IS a valid failure_action.
q: True or false: 3 of 10 updated tasks failing (30%) against max_failure_ratio 0.2 with failure_action rollback reverts the service.

explain: True. --prune garbage-collects the stack's SERVICES (and networks left unused) that the new file no longer declares — it exists precisely because plain stack deploy never deletes, only converges. Volumes, configs, and secrets are not stack-prune targets.
q: True or false: stack deploy --prune removes orphaned SERVICES (and unused networks) — never volumes, configs, or secrets.

explain: True. Three states: active (normal), pause (no new tasks, running ones stay), drain (evict everything, reschedule elsewhere) — items 878/953's distinction. The blip came from mass eviction; the controlled pattern is one node at a time.
q: True or false: Node availability pause blocks NEW placements but leaves running tasks; drain actively evicts and reschedules them.

explain: True. Constraints are hard filters (node must match); placement preferences are soft spread hints — spread=node.labels.rack tells the scheduler to distribute tasks across distinct rack values as evenly as possible (item 803's preference). Update parallelism controls rollout batching, not placement.
q: True or false: --placement-pref 'spread=node.labels.rack' spreads tasks across racks (soft); constraints are hard filters, not spreaders.

domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry
explain: True. Docker's ignore matcher can't descend into an excluded directory to re-include a child — the parent exclusion wins. The fix is granular exclusion (data/* then !data/seed.csv) or re-including the dir first. COPY respects .dockerignore exactly like ADD does.
q: True or false: !data/seed.csv can't re-include a file inside excluded data/ — re-include the directory first (or exclude data/*).

domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry
explain: --target sets the final stage of the build: everything up to and including that stage is built, and that stage's filesystem IS the resulting image (item 856's flag). It's the standard way to extract build-stage artifacts in CI — the engineer got exactly what the flag promises.
options: All stages are produced; --target filters tags
--target stops the build AT the named stage and that stage's image is the result — builder deliberately yields the toolchain image; target final (or omit) for the small one
q: docker build --target builder yields a 900MB toolchain image, not the small final one. What does --target actually do?

domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry
explain: False. save preserves exactly the tags the image had at save time; it can't invent tags. The isolated host failed because app:latest was never created — tag before saving or retag after load.
q: True or false: docker save invents a latest tag on load if the image lacks one.

domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry
explain: True. Immutable tags are a supply-chain guardrail: a tag, once pushed, can't be repointed — defeating tag-mutation attacks (items 731/843/958's policy). The compatible CI pattern is unique tags per build (semver/SHA), with promotion or mutable-tag repos for floating names; there is no --force override.
q: True or false: With MSR immutable tags, CI must push unique tags per build (semver/SHA).

domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry
explain: True. Notary/DCT trust metadata is attached per repository TAG: pushing 1.0 with DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST=1 signs tag 1.0 only. The 2.0 failure means that tag was pushed unsigned (DCT off, different job, or delegation gap) — per-tag scoping is the whole lesson.
q: True or false: DCT trust is per-TAG — app:1.0 signed says nothing about app:2.0, which fails enforcement if pushed unsigned.

explain: True. default-address-pools redefines the CIDR space for networks Docker auto-creates (docker0, user-defined bridges, Swarm overlays) — but only for networks created AFTER the change (item 960's pools; distinct from Swarm's init-time --default-addr-pool). Existing networks keep their subnets until recreated.
q: True or false: daemon.json default-address-pools changes ranges for NEW networks only — existing networks keep their subnets until recreated.

explain: True. MKE 3.x is a dual-orchestrator platform: Swarm and Kubernetes run side by side, and the workload's tooling selects the target (item 828's bundle). That's why the client bundle contains both a Swarm client cert and a kubeconfig. Neither side is a shim for the other.
q: True or false: MKE 3 runs BOTH orchestrators — stack deploy targets Swarm, kubectl targets Kubernetes, on the same cluster.

explain: Daemon default-ulimits sets the baseline ulimits for all containers created afterward — the fleet-wide fix (item 887's daemon side). Host limits.conf is irrelevant because containers inherit the DAEMON's limits, not the host shell's, and the mechanism works for standalone containers, not just Swarm.
options: "default-ulimits": {"nofile": {"Hard": 65536, "Soft": 65536}} in daemon.json — the default for every new container; an explicit --ulimit still overrides per container
q: --ulimit nofile fixes 'too many open files' per container; 200 services need it fleet-wide. Daemon-level setting?

explain: True. Notary delegations are the least-privilege signing pattern: the repo's root key certifies a delegate key for the repository, and that delegate signs pushes (item 832's signer add). Verifiers follow the chain root → delegate; revocation is signer remove, per-repository, not per-tag.
q: True or false: trust signer add delegates signing for a repo WITHOUT exposing the root key — revocable anytime via signer remove.

explain: False. Port publishing is part of the service spec: docker service update --publish-add adds it as a rolling update honoring update_config — no recreate, no downtime.
q: True or false: Adding a second published port to a live service requires removing and recreating it.

explain: True. Aliases (like the automatic service-name alias) live in the embedded DNS PER NETWORK (items 310/866's scoping). Scoping is what makes the design work: one logical name, different backends per network segment. There is no global alias registry to collide in.
q: True or false: Network aliases are scoped PER NETWORK — 'cache' can mean redis on net-a and memcached on net-b simultaneously.

explain: VXLAN encapsulation adds ~50 bytes of overhead — a 1500-byte container MTU produces 1550-byte underlay frames that the 1400-MTU VPN drops (often without ICMP feedback — a PMTU black hole). Jumbo frames make it worse, MTU is a network property (not a docker run flag), and no auto-negotiation saves you through a tunnel.
options: VXLAN adds ~50B overhead: 1500B container frames become 1550B underlay frames the 1400-MTU VPN drops (PMTU black hole) — create the overlay with --opt com.docker.network.driver.mtu=1350 so frames fit after encapsulation
MTU auto-negotiates — it's a firewall rule
q: Overlay traffic crosses a 1400-MTU VPN: large responses hang, small requests work. Mechanism and fix?

explain: True. Swarm separates control (--advertise-addr) from data (--data-path-addr): the data-path address is the interface VXLAN traffic uses (item 768's flag family). Port stays --data-path-port (default UDP 4789); there is no interface benchmarking.
q: True or false: --data-path-addr steers VXLAN onto the fast NIC independently of --advertise-addr; the PORT stays --data-path-port (4789).

explain: Docker happily runs numeric UIDs with no passwd entry — the kernel doesn't care. Userland does: getpwuid()-dependent libraries (Java, some Go libs, NSS) fail, and root-owned files stay root-owned. Dockerfile USER is honored from registries exactly like local builds.
options: Numeric UIDs are invalid — USER needs a name

Numeric USER 1001 is VALID — the container runs as uid 1001; with no /etc/passwd entry, getpwuid() calls fail and root-owned COPY'd files may be unreadable. Fix: useradd in the Dockerfile or chown files to 1001
--user at run overrides; Dockerfile USER is ignored from registries
q: USER 1001: app fails 'no matching entry in passwd'; COPY'd files unreadable. Engineer: 'numeric UIDs are invalid.' Actual rules?

explain: False. Enforcement is SERVER-side on the registry: the repo policy rejects unsigned pushes regardless of client settings. CI must push with DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST=1 (or otherwise sign) so tags carry signatures.
q: True or false: MSR 'require signed images' is enforced client-side by each node's daemon setting.

explain: True. User namespaces are a privilege-containment boundary: they convert 'root in container' into 'unprivileged on host' (items 821/911's mapping), so the highest-value escape outcome (host root) is off the table. The honest caveat: defense-in-depth, not a sandbox — kernel exploits and --privileged still escalate.
q: True or false: With userns-remap, an escaped container-root lands as an UNPRIVILEGED host UID — containment, not a complete sandbox.

explain: Environment is the leakiest secret channel: visible in docker inspect to every API consumer, often logged, committed to repos, and inherited by child processes. 'Only root' ignores the real threat model — the Docker API's audience is root-EQUIVALENT, not root-only, and blast radius is the point. Env files are plaintext too.
options: docker inspect exposes env to ANYONE with API access (CI jobs, monitoring, a compromised container with socket access), and the value sits in the shared repo — use a Swarm secret or external store injected at runtime, never plaintext -e
It's fine — docker access implies root
Env vars are encrypted; inspect shows ciphertext
Move it to --env-file — env files are encrypted
q: docker inspect exposes a DB password passed via -e. Why is 'only root can docker' no defense; what's the proper channel?

explain: --volumes-from replays the source container's volume mounts into the new container — no copying, just shared references, which means the data's availability is coupled to the source container existing. It works with named volumes and binds alike.
options: It copies data at start — safe but slow

--volumes-from works but is LEGACY: it shares the source's MOUNTS (no copy), coupling you to the source container's lifecycle. Modern pattern: named volumes mounted explicitly into each container (-v shared:/data on both)
q: A legacy runbook shares data with --volumes-from. Standardize on it?

explain: 'Reclaimable' = not referenced by any container — but 'unreferenced' includes that critical quarterly-report image (item 934's usage rule). -v gives the per-object breakdown so cleanup is informed; build cache is usually the bulk and the safest first target.
options: Only a daemon restart frees it
Reclaimable means safe — run image prune -a
docker system df -v for the per-image/container/volume breakdown, then prune surgically: builder prune first (usually the bulk), then image prune -a --filter until=/label filters — not a blind -a
q: system df shows 60GB 'reclaimable' under Images; image prune -a might kill a rare-but-critical image. Safer sequence?

explain: True. Union filesystems (overlay2 et al.) are the whole point: the image's layers are mounted read-only and SHARED; each container gets a private writable top layer where only its changes live (copy-up on write). No default compression explains it, and the sharing is on-disk layer references, not RAM dedup.
q: True or false: 100 containers from one 2GB image use ~2GB + thin writable layers — layers are SHARED read-only via copy-on-write.

explain: Mountpoint from docker volume inspect is genuinely useful for forensics, but live mutation races the app — the same torn-write problem as live DB file copies (item 948's consistency rule). The _data directory is the real data (edits DO land), and the daemon doesn't block the path — it's discipline, not enforcement.
options: Recommended — direct edits are the primary method

It works but is UNSUPPORTED while mounted: live edits race app writes (torn files, corrupt DBs); inspect the mountpoint for debugging, mutate via a helper container with the app stopped/quiesced — and never treat the path layout as a stable API
_data is a symlink farm — edits don't land
Direct edits are blocked by the daemon
q: Editing /var/lib/docker/volumes/myvol/_data directly while the app runs 'works and is faster'. A colleague endorses it. Guidance?

explain: True. Unlock-key rotation re-keys the Raft encryption: the old key immediately stops working for any FUTURE unlock (item 876's key lifecycle). Running, unlocked managers don't notice — they're already decrypted in memory; locked managers keep their data, they just need the new key.
q: True or false: After swarm unlock-key --rotate, a later-locked manager needs the NEW key — the old key is invalid cluster-wide.

explain: True. Swarm keeps a bounded history of task attempts per slot (default 5) — that's what service ps renders. Shutdown/Failed rows are forensic records; the actual containers are typically already removed by the daemon, and history rolls over rather than growing forever.
q: True or false: service ps shows task HISTORY (--task-history-limit, default 5 per slot) — Shutdown/Failed rows are records, not runnable containers.

explain: Swarm exposes node.platform.os and node.platform.arch as built-in node attributes — the correct selector for OS-specific images (Windows containers need Windows nodes and vice versa). Hostname constraints don't glob, and placement preferences are soft — they can't enforce a hard OS requirement.
options: Mixed-OS swarms can't constrain by OS
--constraint 'node.platform.os==linux' — platform constraints match the node's OS/arch; hostnames are brittle (nodes get replaced) while platform is intrinsic, engine-maintained
q: Linux-only image tasks keep landing on Windows nodes in a mixed-OS swarm. Constraint — without hardcoding hostnames?

explain: True. docker login authenticates ONE daemon. stack deploy ships the service spec to all nodes, but the registry credential only travels with it under --with-registry-auth — the classic 'works on the manager, unauthorized on workers' trap. Workers never need individual logins for stack pulls.
q: True or false: Private-image stacks fail on workers without stack deploy --with-registry-auth — login on the manager alone doesn't forward credentials.

domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry
explain: ADD's two extras are exactly the surprises: local archive auto-extraction and URL fetching. Because they're implicit, the Dockerfile best-practice guidance is COPY-first — explicit beats clever. (COPY also copies from the build context only; neither instruction reaches outside it except ADD's URL fetch.)
options: ADD has magic: auto-extracts local archives and fetches remote URLs; COPY does neither — local files verbatim. Best practice: COPY by default, ADD only when you explicitly want extraction or URL fetching
q: ADD app.tar.gz extracts into /opt/ instead of copying; ADD <url> fetches remotely. When ADD vs COPY — the rule?

domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry
explain: True. Layer cache invalidation is positional: a changed layer invalidates everything beneath it. Dependencies change rarely, code changes constantly — so the manifest copy + install must sit ABOVE the code copy. --no-cache throws away the mechanism instead of arranging it.
q: True or false: COPY package*.json + npm ci BEFORE COPY . — a changed layer invalidates all layers after it.

domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry
explain: True. A tag is a mutable nickname; a digest is the image's content hash. image:tag@digest says 'this tag, AND exactly these bits' — the deploy becomes immune to tag mutation (item 895's integrity half). Digests work identically on private registries.
q: True or false: Freeze a deploy's meaning by pinning the DIGEST (app:1.4.2@sha256:...) — tags are mutable pointers, digests are content-addressed.

domain: Domain 2: Image Creation, Management, and Registry
explain: False. With credsStore configured, the secret lives in the OS credential store (keychain/helper); config.json holds only the store's NAME. CI needs its own docker login or a helper available there.
q: True or false: Copying config.json to CI carries the Docker Hub credential with it.

explain: MKE manages its own node lifecycle: the UI-issued token drives MKE's join bundle (which installs the agent, registers the node with both orchestrators, and applies labels). A raw docker swarm join would enroll the node in the underlying swarm while bypassing everything that makes it an MKE node.
options: Nothing — MKE tokens are standard Swarm tokens

MKE's join isn't raw swarm join: the UI provides a join command/script enrolling the node through MKE (agent install, labels, orchestrator registration) — the token is consumed by MKE's flow, not the Swarm CLI
q: Joining a worker to MKE with the UI token via plain docker swarm join fails. What's wrong with the approach?

explain: True. /var/lib/docker/<driver>/ is per-driver: overlay2's layers are meaningless to devicemapper and vice versa (items 741/850's rule). The data still sits on disk under the old driver's directory — invisible, not destroyed — and switching back restores access.
q: True or false: Switching storage drivers makes old data INVISIBLE, not deleted — each driver keeps its own tree under /var/lib/docker.

explain: Docker has first-class zfs (and btrfs) drivers selected daemon-wide in daemon.json — but the filesystem must exist on the host; there's no auto-detection from the root fs. The zfs driver maps Docker's layer model onto datasets, which is exactly the native behavior wanted.
options: "storage-driver": "zfs" in daemon.json (ZFS present on the host) — a dataset per layer/container, ZFS snapshots/compression semantics; trade-off: only works where ZFS exists, and switching orphans the overlay2 data
Docker auto-detects ZFS — overlay2 means ZFS is absent
q: A ZFS host (datasets, snapshots, compression) got overlay2 by default. The team wants the zfs driver. Configuration and constraints?

explain: True. docker logs reads the daemon's LOCAL log files — which only exist for json-file/local drivers (items 348/814's limitation). Third-party drivers ship logs off-host and keep no local copy; that's by design, not breakage. Dual logging (20.10+) is the bridge when both are needed.
q: True or false: With gelf/syslog drivers, docker logs returns nothing — only json-file/local keep local copies.

explain: True. Engine version management is the OS package manager's job: apt-get install docker-ce=<version> style pins (exact strings from apt-cache madison), plus holds/pinning so unattended upgrades don't drift the host out of support (item 936's matrix). The preflight check is a hard requirement, not advisory.
q: True or false: Pin Engine to MKE's supported release at install (apt pin + hold).

explain: docker network connect/disconnect mutate a RUNNING container's network attachments live: new veth, new IP, DNS updated — the standard 'oops, need another network' fix. (For Swarm services, the equivalent is service update --network-add.) Networks are creation-fixed only if you never use the connect verb.
options: Impossible — networks are fixed at creation
docker network connect backend <container> — hot-attaches an interface: new IP, DNS entries, aliases immediately, no restart; network disconnect reverses it live
connect works only on stopped containers
q: A running debug container on frontend must reach a database on backend — WITHOUT restarting it. Correct operation, and what changes?

Docker's default IPAM hands out from the same default pools, so uncoordinated network create calls CAN collide — and identical subnets on two overlays produce genuinely ambiguous routing (same destination, two networks). Encryption separates traffic cryptographically, not address spaces.
q: True or false: Overlapping overlay subnets cause cross-network misrouting — assign explicit non-overlapping --subnet per network, coordinated with the IPAM plan.

explain: True. The Swarm port trinity: 2377/TCP for manager API and Raft, 7946 TCP+UDP for gossip (failure detection, network state), 4789/UDP for VXLAN data. Encrypted overlays add IPsec (ESP, protocol 50). 2376 is the TLS daemon port — a different surface entirely.
q: True or false: Between Swarm nodes: 2377/TCP (management/Raft), 7946 TCP+UDP (gossip), 4789/UDP (VXLAN) — plus ESP (proto 50) if overlays are encrypted.

explain: docker service logs is the aggregate view (multiplexed, with task-name prefixes) — it deliberately has no task filter. The per-task view is docker logs against the specific container on its node. --tail limits line count across the aggregate; it doesn't select a task.
options: service logs aggregates across tasks with NO per-task filter — find the task's node (service ps) and run docker logs <container-id> there

q: True or false: MKE collection grants are hierarchical — a grant on /Prod covers /Prod/Web.

explain: False. --external-ca is an init/join-time directive — node certs get signed by the external CA instead of the built-in one. An existing swarm can't be retrofitted; it would need recreation (or keep its own CA, the normal supported posture).
q: True or false: An existing swarm can switch to the corporate CA anytime with swarm ca --rotate --external-ca.

explain: --privileged is three things at once: all capabilities, all host devices, and confinement profiles lifted. Decomposing it: capabilities for the syscalls (--cap-add), devices for the hardware (--device), profiles left at defaults. Containers capture packets fine unprivileged with NET_RAW; devices were never 'unrestricted' — the device cgroup is exactly what --device opens selectively.
options: Run the agent on the host instead

--cap-add=NET_RAW --cap-add=NET_ADMIN --device=/dev/bus/usb (plus specific device nodes) — --privileged grants ALL capabilities, ALL host devices, and lifts seccomp/AppArmor; the targeted flags reproduce only the needed pieces
q: A monitoring agent 'needs --privileged' for packet capture + USB devices. Least-privilege equivalent, and what does --privileged actually grant?

explain: Two different 'driver' concepts: STORAGE drivers (overlay2) = how container layers are stored; VOLUME drivers/plugins = how named volumes are provisioned — and plugins are Docker's extensibility point for external systems (items 825/848's architecture). REX-Ray preempts (force-detaches) precisely BECAUSE volumes move with rescheduled tasks.
options: Volume plugins ARE the driver mechanism for network/cloud storage: the plugin implements the volume driver API, so -d rexray/ebs provisions real EBS volumes per task; PREEMPT lets a rescheduled task force-detach from the old node. A storage DRIVER (overlay2) is a different layer — the container filesystem
rex-ray is a storage driver; -d aliases --storage-driver
q: REX-Ray plugin installed; volume create -d rexray/ebs works. Why a PLUGIN and not a storage driver — the architecture?

explain: True. Two classic NFS gotchas in one: (1) version negotiation — a v4-only server rejects the client's default v3 attempt, so pinning vers=4 among the mount options is required; (2) root squash maps container root to nobody on the server (items 874/922's mount, version-pinned). device= carries the export path; addr= remains the server option.
q: True or false: NFS mounts failing 'permission denied' on a v4-only server usually miss vers=4 in the options.

explain: True. The populate-on-first-use behavior is a named-volume-only feature (items 396/898's seeding): docker run -v myvol:/app/data on an empty myvol seeds it from the image — the standard 'ship default configs in the image, let users customize' pattern. Bind mounts shadow the path with the host directory as-is, always.
q: True or false: Named volumes are seeded from image content only when empty; existing data is never overwritten.

explain: True. Per-container filesystem quotas are driver-dependent: devicemapper/zfs/btrfs implement size= natively; overlay2 can only enforce it via XFS project quotas (the pquota mount flag on the backing fs) — item 897's backend rule. --ulimit fsize caps single FILE size, a different knob entirely.
q: True or false: --storage-opt size= works on devicemapper/zfs/btrfs natively; on overlay2 it needs XFS + pquota — ext4-backed overlay2 rejects it.

explain: True. docker cp is the daemon-mediated tar pipe: CONTAINER:PATH addressing both directions, any container state, no volume or exec prerequisites (items 300/592/795's utility). Into the container = writes to the writable layer (or the mounted volume, if the path is a mount).
q: True or false: docker cp works on running containers, needs no volume, and writes land in the writable layer.
